questions.title: Intersecting domain restrictions
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(16-4x^2-y^2)+\dfrac{\sqrt{y-x^2}}{x-1}\). (a) Describe the domain using simultaneous inequalities. (b) Sketch the domain, distinguishing included and excluded boundaries. (c) Which points belong to the domain: \((0,0),\ (1,2),\ (0,4),\ (-1,2)\)?

blocks: The region lies inside the ellipse and on or above the parabola, with the line \(x=1\) removed. The ellipse is excluded; the feasible part of the parabola is included.
Only \((0,0)\) and \((-1,2)\) belong to the domain.
answer.text: \(D=\{(x,y):4x^2+y^2<16,\ y\ge x^2,\ x\ne1\}\). The region lies inside the ellipse and on or above the parabola, with the line \(x=1\) removed. The ellipse is excluded; the feasible part of the parabola is included. Only \((0,0)\) and \((-1,2)\) belong to the domain.

questions.title: Surface and horizontal sections
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=\sqrt{16-4x^2-y^2}\). (a) Find the domain and range. (b) Identify the graph as a familiar surface, including the restriction on \(z\). (c) Describe the level curves for \(k=0,2,4,5\), giving axis intercepts when appropriate.

blocks: The graph is the upper half of the ellipsoid \(4x^2+y^2+z^2=16\), with \(z\ge0\).
For \(k=2\): \(4x^2+y^2=12\), intercepts \((\pm\sqrt3,0),(0,\pm2\sqrt3)\).
For \(k=4\): only \((0,0)\). For \(k=5\): empty.
answer.text: Domain: \(4x^2+y^2\le16\). Range: \([0,4]\). The graph is the upper half of the ellipsoid \(4x^2+y^2+z^2=16\), with \(z\ge0\). For \(k=0\): \(4x^2+y^2=16\), intercepts \((\pm2,0),(0,\pm4)\). For \(k=2\): \(4x^2+y^2=12\), intercepts \((\pm\sqrt3,0),(0,\pm2\sqrt3)\). For \(k=4\): only \((0,0)\). For \(k=5\): empty.

body: (a) Find the domain and range.
(b) Identify the graph as a familiar surface, including the restriction on \(z\).
(c) Describe the level curves for \(k=0,2,4,5\), giving axis intercepts when appropriate.

questions.title: Shifted saddle contours
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=(y-1)^2-(x+2)^2\). Sketch the level curves for \(k=-4,0,4\). Identify their center and orientations, and describe the regions where \(f\) is positive or negative.

blocks: For \(k=4\), the hyperbola opens in the \(y\)-direction, with vertices \((-2,3),(-2,-1)\).
For \(k=-4\), it opens in the \(x\)-direction, with vertices \((0,1),(-4,1)\).
Positive where \(|y-1|>|x+2|\); negative where \(|y-1|<|x+2|\).
answer.text: Center: \((-2,1)\). For \(k=4\), the hyperbola opens in the \(y\)-direction, with vertices \((-2,3),(-2,-1)\). For \(k=-4\), it opens in the \(x\)-direction, with vertices \((0,1),(-4,1)\). For \(k=0\): \(y-1=\pm(x+2)\). Positive where \(|y-1|>|x+2|\); negative where \(|y-1|<|x+2|\).

questions.title: Reading contour spacing
questions.text: The two contour maps below show levels \(k=1,2,3,4\). One represents \(f(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+4y^2}\); the other represents \(g(x,y)=x^2+4y^2\). (a) Match each function to its contour map. (b) For each function, find the positive \(x\)-intercepts of the \(k=2\) and \(k=3\) level curves and their separation. (c) Identify each graph and explain how the contour spacing reflects its radial growth.

blocks: Map A represents \(f\), an upper elliptic cone. Its positive intercepts are \(2\) and \(3\), separated by \(1\).
Map B represents \(g\), an elliptic paraboloid. Its positive intercepts are \(\sqrt2\) and \(\sqrt3\), separated by \(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\).
Map A has constant spacing for equal height steps. Map B has decreasing spacing as the level increases, reflecting faster outward growth.
answer.text: Map A represents \(f\), an upper elliptic cone. Its positive intercepts are \(2\) and \(3\), separated by \(1\). Map B represents \(g\), an elliptic paraboloid. Its positive intercepts are \(\sqrt2\) and \(\sqrt3\), separated by \(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\). Map A has constant spacing for equal height steps. Map B has decreasing spacing as the level increases, reflecting faster outward growth.

questions.title: Temperature threshold
questions.text: Let \(T(x,y)=\dfrac{120}{1+x^2+4y^2}\). (a) Find the range. (b) Describe the isotherms \(T=60\) and \(T=24\). (c) Describe the region where the temperature is at least \(24\). (d) Is a temperature of \(0\) attained?

blocks: The temperature approaches \(0\) but never equals \(0\).
answer.text: Range: \((0,120]\). \(T=60\): \(x^2+4y^2=1\). \(T=24\): \(x^2+4y^2=4\). \(T\ge24\) where \(x^2+4y^2\le4\). The temperature approaches \(0\) but never equals \(0\).

body: (a) Find the range.
(b) Describe the isotherms \(T=60\) and \(T=24\).

questions.title: Range after restricting the inputs
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(y-x^2)\), with the additional restriction \(y\le4\). Find the domain, its projection onto the \(x\)-axis, and the range. Find the maximum and all points where it occurs. Does a smallest value exist? Justify your answer.

blocks: Domain: \(x^2<y\le4\). Projection: \(-2<x<2\).
Range: \((-\infty,\ln4]\). The maximum is \(\ln4\), attained only at \((0,4)\).
There is no minimum: \(\ln(y-x^2)\to-\infty\) as \(y-x^2\to0^+\).
answer.text: Domain: \(x^2<y\le4\). Projection: \(-2<x<2\). Range: \((-\infty,\ln4]\). The maximum is \(\ln4\), attained only at \((0,4)\). There is no minimum: \(\ln(y-x^2)\to-\infty\) as \(y-x^2\to0^+\).

body: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(y-x^2)\), with the additional restriction \(y\le4\).

questions.title: A parameter changes the entire surface
questions.text: Let \(f_a(x,y)=\sqrt{a-x^2-y^2}\). Classify the domain and range for \(a<0,\ a=0,\ a>0\). When \(a>0\), classify the level sets as circles, a single point, or empty.

blocks: If \(a<0\), the domain and range are empty.
If \(a=0\), the domain is \(\{(0,0)\}\) and the range is \(\{0\}\).
If \(a>0\), the domain is \(x^2+y^2\le a\) and the range is \([0,\sqrt a]\).
For \(0\le k<\sqrt a\), the level curve is the circle \(x^2+y^2=a-k^2\). For \(k=\sqrt a\), it is \((0,0)\). All other levels are empty.
answer.text: If \(a<0\), the domain and range are empty. If \(a=0\), the domain is \(\{(0,0)\}\) and the range is \(\{0\}\). If \(a>0\), the domain is \(x^2+y^2\le a\) and the range is \([0,\sqrt a]\). For \(0\le k<\sqrt a\), the level curve is the circle \(x^2+y^2=a-k^2\). For \(k=\sqrt a\), it is \((0,0)\). All other levels are empty.

body: Let \(f_a(x,y)=\sqrt{a-x^2-y^2}\).
Classify the domain and range for \(a<0,\ a=0,\ a>0\). When \(a>0\), classify the level sets as circles, a single point, or empty.

\(f_y=x^3e^{xy}+\ln(x+y)+\dfrac{y}{x+y}\).

questions.title: Quotient and equal trace slopes
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x+y}\). Find \(f_x,f_y,f_{xx},f_{xy},f_{yy}\). At which points in the domain are the two coordinate slopes equal?

blocks: \(f_x=\dfrac{y^2}{(x+y)^2},\quad f_y=\dfrac{x^2}{(x+y)^2}\).
\(f_{xx}=-\dfrac{2y^2}{(x+y)^3},\quad f_{xy}=\dfrac{2xy}{(x+y)^3},\quad f_{yy}=-\dfrac{2x^2}{(x+y)^3}\).
The domain excludes \(x+y=0\). Equal slopes occur at \((t,t)\), with \(t\ne0\).

blocks: Equality of mixed partials requires \(2x+2y=2x+ay\), so \(a=2\).

questions.title: Partial derivatives versus continuity
questions.text: Define \(f(x,y)=\dfrac{xy}{x^2+y^2}\) away from the origin, and \(f(0,0)=0\). Use the definitions to find both partial derivatives at the origin. Test continuity along \(y=0\) and \(y=x\). Is the function differentiable at the origin, and does it have a valid linear approximation there?

blocks: Along \(y=0\), the limit is \(0\); along \(y=x\), it is \(\tfrac12\).
The function is not continuous, hence not differentiable, at the origin. It has no valid linear approximation there.
answer.text: \(f_x(0,0)=f_y(0,0)=0\). Along \(y=0\), the limit is \(0\); along \(y=x\), it is \(\tfrac12\). The function is not continuous, hence not differentiable, at the origin. It has no valid linear approximation there.

questions.text: A cylinder has diameter \(10\) cm and height \(12\) cm. The maximum measurement errors are \(0.04\) cm in diameter and \(0.03\) cm in height. Estimate the maximum absolute and percentage volume errors. If only one error can be halved, which choice reduces the estimated error more, and by how much?

blocks: Maximum absolute error: \(3.15\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}\). Percentage error: \(1.05\%\).
Halving the diameter error reduces the estimate by \(1.2\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}\); halving the height error reduces it by \(0.375\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}\).
Halving the diameter error gives the greater reduction, by \(0.825\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3}\).

questions.title: A contour map with a restricted domain
body: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(y-x^2)\) on its natural domain. Find the domain and range. Write the level curves for \(k=-1,0,1\), including their vertices.
As \(k\) increases, which way do the curves move? At fixed \(x\), do equal increases in \(k\) produce equal vertical spacing? Find the vertical separations between these three curves.
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(y-x^2)\) on its natural domain. Find the domain and range. Write the level curves for \(k=-1,0,1\), including their vertices. As \(k\) increases, which way do the curves move? At fixed \(x\), do equal increases in \(k\) produce equal vertical spacing? Find the vertical separations between these three curves.

blocks: Upward; spacing increases. Separations: \(1-e^{-1}\) and \(e-1\).
answer.text: Domain: \(y>x^2\). Range: \(\mathbb R\). Levels: \(y=x^2+e^{-1}\), \(y=x^2+1\), \(y=x^2+e\); vertices \((0,e^{-1}),(0,1),(0,e)\). Upward; spacing increases. Separations: \(1-e^{-1}\) and \(e-1\).

questions.title: Recover a surface from its level curves

Find the level through \((4,2)\), its vertex, and the trace in the plane \(x=1\). Give the domain and range.
questions.text: A function has level curve \(y=(x-1)^2+2-3k\) at height \(k\), for every real \(k\). Recover \(f(x,y)\) and identify its three-dimensional graph. Find the level through \((4,2)\), its vertex, and the trace in the plane \(x=1\). Give the domain and range.

blocks: \(f(x,y)=\big((x-1)^2+2-y\big)/3\). A parabolic cylinder with ruling direction \(\langle0,-3,1\rangle\). Domain: \(\mathbb R^2\); range: \(\mathbb R\).
answer.text: \(f(x,y)=\big((x-1)^2+2-y\big)/3\). A parabolic cylinder with ruling direction \(\langle0,-3,1\rangle\). Domain: \(\mathbb R^2\); range: \(\mathbb R\). Through \((4,2)\): \(k=3\), \(y=(x-1)^2-7\), vertex \((1,-7)\). Trace: \(x=1\), \(z=(2-y)/3\), a line.

Use that plane to estimate the height at \((2.03,-0.98)\). Find the exact error, actual value minus estimate, and determine whether this tangent plane underestimates the surface everywhere.

blocks: Point \((2,-1,6)\). Plane \(z=4x-4y-6\). Estimate \(6.04\); exact error \(0.0017\).
Yes: the error is \((x-2)^2+2(y+1)^2\ge0\), with equality only at the tangency point.
answer.text: Point \((2,-1,6)\). Plane \(z=4x-4y-6\). Estimate \(6.04\); exact error \(0.0017\). Yes: the error is \((x-2)^2+2(y+1)^2\ge0\), with equality only at the tangency point.

For signed changes \(dx=0.01\) and \(dy=-0.02\), choose \(dz\) so the first-order volume change is zero. Is that choice within its allowed bound? Find the actual volume change for those three signed changes.

blocks: Maximum estimated absolute error: \(0.34\text{ m}^3\). Percentage: \(17/12\%\approx1.4167\%\).

answer.text: Maximum estimated absolute error: \(0.34\text{ m}^3\). Percentage: \(17/12\%\approx1.4167\%\). \(dz=1/150\text{ m}\), within the bound. Actual change: \(-217/250000\text{ m}^3=-0.000868\text{ m}^3\).

A student says the level \(c=-2\) is the same ellipse as \(c=2\), since both give \(x^2+4y^2=5\) after squaring. Is this correct?
questions.text: For \(f(x,y)=\sqrt{9-x^2-4y^2}\), find the domain and range. Describe the level curves for \(c=0,1,2,3\) and give their intercepts (or the single point when applicable). A student says the level \(c=-2\) is the same ellipse as \(c=2\), since both give \(x^2+4y^2=5\) after squaring. Is this correct?

blocks: \(c=3\): the single point \((0,0)\). Level \(c=-2\): empty; the student is incorrect.
answer.text: Domain: \(x^2+4y^2\le9\). Range: \([0,3]\). \(c=0\): \(x^2+4y^2=9\), intercepts \((\pm3,0),(0,\pm3/2)\). \(c=1\): \(x^2+4y^2=8\), intercepts \((\pm2\sqrt2,0),(0,\pm\sqrt2)\). \(c=2\): \(x^2+4y^2=5\), intercepts \((\pm\sqrt5,0),(0,\pm\sqrt5/2)\). \(c=3\): the single point \((0,0)\). Level \(c=-2\): empty; the student is incorrect.

questions.title: Top-down design
body: Which decomposition best follows top-down design for a study-session analyzer?
choices: Create separate tasks for each line of Python syntax.
Choose every variable name before identifying the major tasks.
Read sessions; answer queries; report results. Then refine each task.
Write one large loop, then divide it into equal-length pieces.

blocks: C. Read sessions; answer queries; report results. Then refine each task.
Start with the overall goal, identify coherent major responsibilities, and refine them until implementation is clear. Equal size or shared syntax does not make a coherent task.
Source: L8 pp11-18

questions.title: Hierarchies
body: A design tree has root R with children A and B. A has children C and D; B has no children. Which statement is correct?
choices: B, C, and D are leaves; A is the parent of C and D.
Only C and D are leaves.
Every node must have exactly two children.
R has no children because it is the root.

blocks: A. B, C, and D are leaves; A is the parent of C and D.
A leaf has no children, even when it is closer to the root than other leaves. The root has no parent, not no children.
Source: L8 p13

questions.title: Design judgment
body: Which claim about top-down design agrees with the lecture?
choices: Several decompositions can be reasonable; hierarchies may miss cross-connections.
Every problem has exactly one correct design tree.
Stop only when every node corresponds to exactly one line of code.
A hierarchy captures every relationship in a system.

blocks: A. Several decompositions can be reasonable; hierarchies may miss cross-connections.
The lecture allows multiple designs and notes artificial boundaries and uncaptured relationships. Stop when implementation is obvious, not at a rigid line count.
Source: L8 pp14-18

body: What is printed?

blocks: Updating an existing key does not add a pair. C stores 9 when assigned; changing B afterward does not recalculate C.

questions.title: Dictionary membership
body: Which expression is True?
choices: "ab" in d and 3 not in d

blocks: B. "ab" in d and 3 not in d
Dictionary membership checks exact keys. It neither searches substrings inside keys nor searches values. Repeated values are allowed.
Source: L8 pp28,31-32

body: What happens?

blocks: D. Prints 7 9, then raises KeyError
Integer 0 and string "0" are different keys. d[0] is a lookup by key, not a request for the first entry.
Source: L8 pp29-31

body: What is printed?

blocks: Initialize each key only on its first encounter. Every occurrence adds 2. len counts distinct keys, not iterations.
Source: L8 pp29-32 plus L6 loops

questions.title: Dictionary traversal
body: What is printed?

blocks: The loop variable receives keys. Updating values for existing keys is allowed; the updated values 3 and 5 contribute to total.
Source: L8 pp30-32

questions.title: Definition versus execution
body: What is printed?

blocks: A definition does not execute its body. The undefined function is inside an uncalled body, so it is never looked up.
Source: L9 pp39-51

questions.title: Print versus return
body: What is printed? The symbol / in the choices means a new line.

body.code:
def double(x):
    print(x * 2)
y = double(3)
print(y)

blocks: B. 6 / None
The inner print displays 6. Because double reaches its end without return, its returned value is None, which is assigned to y and then printed.

questions.title: Immediate return
body: What is printed?

blocks: return exits the entire function at the first match. The final return handles the no-match case only after the loop finishes.
Source: L9 pp81-84 plus L6

questions.title: Tuple return and unpacking
body: What is printed?

body.code:
def parts(a, b):
    return a // b, a % b
r, q = parts(17, 5)
print(r, q, r + q)

blocks: The function returns one tuple (3,2). Unpacking follows position, regardless of whether the caller uses conventional quotient/remainder names.
Source: L9 pp14-21

questions.title: Defaults
body: What is printed?

blocks: Provided positional arguments fill from left to right; omitted trailing arguments use their defaults. Zero is supplied explicitly, so it does not trigger a default.
Source: L9 pp85-88

questions.title: Function headers
body: Which header is invalid for the ordinary positional parameters taught in the slides?

blocks: A. def f(a=1, b):
A required positional parameter cannot follow one with a default. This is a syntax error in the definition, not an error postponed until calling.
Source: L9 pp85-88

questions.title: Local state
body: What is printed?

body.code:
def bump(a):
    a += 3
    return a
a = 5
b = bump(a)
print(a, b, bump(b))

blocks: Each call has its own parameter binding. Reassigning a numeric parameter does not change the caller variable. The returned value matters only where it is used.
Source: L9 pp65-78,81

questions.title: Reading global state
body: What is printed?

body.code:
rate = 2
def cost(n):
    return n * rate
rate = 3
print(cost(4))

blocks: With no local rate assignment, the function reads the global rate when called. It does not freeze rate at definition time. Passing rate as an argument would make the dependency clearer.
Source: L9 pp63-64

questions.title: Assignment and scope
body: What happens?

body.code:
score = 10
def add():
    score += 2
    return score
print(add())

blocks: C. UnboundLocalError before any output
+= is assignment. Without a parameter, local initialization, or global declaration, score is treated as local but read before receiving a value.
Source: L9 p77

questions.title: Explicit global
body: What is printed?

body.code:
count = 1
def step():
    global count
    count += 2
    return count
a = step()
b = step()
print(a, b, count)

blocks: global allows assignment to the main-program count. The first return stores 3 in a; the later change to count does not alter a. Prefer explicit parameters and returns in new designs.
Source: L9 pp79-80

questions.title: Mutation then rebinding
body: What is printed?

body.code:
def change(a):
    a[0] = 9
    a = [4, 5]
    a[1] = 8
    return a
x = [1, 2]
y = change(x)
print(x, y)

blocks: The first element assignment mutates the shared original list. Rebinding local a to a new list separates later changes; returning that new list gives it to y.
Source: L9 pp97-106

questions.title: List += versus +
body: What is printed?

body.code:
def extend(a, b):
    a += [7]
    b = b + [8]
x = [1]
y = [2]
extend(x, y)
print(x, y)

blocks: For lists, += extends the shared object. b + [8] builds a new list and b = rebinds only the local parameter.
Source: L9 pp90-98

questions.title: Copies and aliases
body: What is printed?

blocks: a and b refer to one list. The slice makes a separate outer list; its numeric entries can be replaced independently.
Source: L9 p107

questions.title: Tuple containing a list
body: What happens? / means a new line.

blocks: A. Prints [9, 2], then raises TypeError
Tuple slots cannot be reassigned, but a list referenced by a slot remains mutable. The tuple still refers to the same list after its contents change.
Source: L9 pp18,99

questions.title: Nested calls
body: What is printed?

blocks: g(3) calls f(3), gets 5, and returns 5*3=15. The outer f then receives 15 and returns 17. Keep a separate x for each invocation.
Source: L9 pp38-50,65-78

questions.title: Dictionary argument
body: What is printed?

blocks: The passed dictionary is mutable. Both updates affect counts, including the new key. Each returned integer is stored separately.
Source: L8 pp29-32; L9 p96

questions.title: Design before coding
body: A program records study sessions (test name, minutes), answers repeated test-name queries, and prints a final summary. Draw or outline a top-down tree with three major tasks and at least two leaf tasks under each. Identify one parent and one leaf. Explain when to stop refining.

blocks: One valid tree: Study analyzer -> Read sessions (read name; validate/read minutes); Answer queries (find matching sessions; calculate count/total); Present final summary (calculate all-session totals; format report). Read sessions is a parent; read name is a leaf. Refine until implementation is clear in a few lines. Other coherent, distinct decompositions are valid.
Rubric: 2 points: coherent major tasks. 2: meaningful refinement. 1: correct parent/leaf identification. 1: stopping criterion.
Source: L8 pp11-22

questions.title: Repair dictionary counting
body: The function should return counts for all words. Identify two logic defects and rewrite it. Example: ["red", "red", "blue"] must produce counts red=2 and blue=1.

blocks: The count resets on every occurrence, and return exits during the first iteration. Initialize only missing keys and return after the loop.
Rubric: 2 points: identify both defects. 2: correct initialization/update. 1: return after loop. 1: empty list returns {}.
Source: L8 pp29-32

questions.title: Separate print from return
body: State the output before failure and the error type. Rewrite area so result becomes 13 for this call, with no printing inside area. Add a one-sentence docstring.

blocks: It prints 12, then raises TypeError because area returns None and None + 1 is invalid. Return the product instead.

blocks.code:
def area(w, h):
    """Return rectangle area for width w and height h."""
    return w * h
result = area(3, 4) + 1

blocks: Rubric: 2 points: 12 then TypeError. 2: return product. 1: meaningful docstring. 1: caller obtains 13 without function output.
Source: L9 pp10-13,81-84

questions.title: Parameter order and tuple results
body: Write split_total(total, people=2) for nonnegative integer total and positive integer people. Return a tuple (equal_share, leftover) using integer division and remainder. Show one call using the default, unpack the result, and give the returned value for split_total(17, 5). Do not print inside the function.

blocks: The default call may use any valid total. split_total(17, 5) returns (3, 2). Unpacking uses the returned order.
Rubric: 1 point: correct default header. 2: // and %. 1: tuple return. 1: default call/unpacking. 1: (3, 2).
Source: L9 pp14-21,85-88

questions.title: Repair scope without global
body: Explain the failure. Rewrite the function and its call so score becomes 12 without global, input, or printing inside the function.

body.code:
score = 10
def increase():
    score += 2
increase()

blocks: Assignment makes score local to increase, but += reads it before any local value exists: UnboundLocalError. Pass the value, return the new value, and assign that return in the caller.

blocks.code:
def increase(score):
    return score + 2
score = 10
score = increase(score)

blocks: Rubric: 2 points: scope explanation. 1: parameter. 1: return. 1: caller assignment. 1: no global.
Source: L9 pp63-80

questions.title: Trace two references
body: Give the final values of x and y. Explain which statement affects the caller. Then change only the call so x stays [2, 4] while y has the same value as before.

body.code:
def edit(a):
    a[0] += 3
    a = a + [9]
    return a
x = [2, 4]
y = edit(x)

blocks: Initially x ends as [5,4] and y as [5,4,9]. a[0] += 3 mutates the shared list; a = a + [9] rebinds the local parameter to a new list. Change the call to y = edit(x[:]) to protect the original list of numbers.
Rubric: 2 points: final values. 2: mutation versus rebinding. 2: slice at call and correct unchanged x.
Source: L9 pp93-107

questions.title: Early return or full scan?
body: This function should return how many values meet the threshold. Explain why it fails, fix only the indentation of return, and give results for tally([8, 2, 9], 5) and tally([], 5).

blocks: return inside the loop stops after the first item, and an empty list reaches the end without a return. Move return count to the same indentation level as for. The corrected results are 2 and 0.
Rubric: 2 points: both failure modes. 2: indentation repair. 2: correct results.
Source: L9 pp81-84; L6 loops

questions.title: Explain tuple immutability precisely
body: Give the values printed. Explain why the list change is visible but the string reassignment is not. Would t[1] = [0] be allowed?

body.code:
name = "A"
scores = [2, 4]
t = (name, scores)
name = "B"
scores[1] = 7
print(t[0], t[1])

blocks: Output: A [2, 7]. The tuple keeps its reference to the original string "A"; rebinding name does not replace the tuple slot. It also keeps a reference to scores, whose contents can change. t[1] = [0] would raise TypeError because it replaces a tuple slot.
Rubric: 2 points: output. 2: distinguish string rebinding and list mutation. 2: reject tuple item assignment with explanation.
Source: L9 pp18,99

questions.title: Study-session query engine

body.code: def analyze_sessions(names, minutes, queries):

body: Aggregate study sessions, then answer queries in their original order. Return a list of tuples (test_name, session_count, total_minutes). Repeated queries must produce repeated results. An unknown test returns a count and total of zero. Do not change any input list.

names and minutes have equal lengths, 0-1000. Names and query strings are case-sensitive; minutes are nonnegative integers. queries has 0-1000 entries. Use a dictionary to aggregate each test once, then answer queries without rescanning all sessions. Use only dictionary indexing/membership, loops, list append, tuples, and ordinary arithmetic; no get/items/values, Counter, comprehensions, or imports.

body.code:
analyze_sessions(["Math", "ENGR", "Math"], [20, 15, 30],
                 ["Math", "Chem", "Math"])
=> [("Math", 2, 50), ("Chem", 0, 0), ("Math", 2, 50)]

analyze_sessions([], [], ["ENGR"])
=> [("ENGR", 0, 0)]

analyze_sessions(["ENGR"], [0], ["ENGR"])
=> [("ENGR", 1, 0)]

body: Write a top-down plan, include a docstring, and test empty inputs and repeated values. Return results; do not print inside the function.
hints: Use each test name as a key and store [count, total] as its value. Initialize a missing name before updating it.
Build a separate output list by looping through queries. For missing names append a zero-result tuple; do not add missing queries to the session data.

blocks: Each input session contributes exactly once. A zero-minute session still counts as one session. Iterating over queries preserves order and duplicates. All modified lists belong to the newly created totals/results structures, so the inputs remain unchanged.

questions.title: First unique reading

body.code: def first_unique(values):

body: Return the tuple (index, value) for the first element whose value occurs exactly once in the entire input list. First means smallest original index, not smallest numeric value. If no unique value exists, return (-1, 0). Do not modify values.

0-1000 integer readings, including negatives and zero. Use a dictionary for frequencies and at most two full passes over values. Do not sort or use list count, dictionary get/items/values, sets, comprehensions, or imports.

body.code:
first_unique([0, 0])
=> (-1, 0)

first_unique([0])
=> (0, 0)

body: Write a top-down plan, include a docstring, and test empty inputs and repeated values. Return results; do not print inside the function.
hints: In your first pass, count every value with a dictionary. A value seen once so far may appear again later.
In a second pass, visit original indices in increasing order. Return at the first count of one; put the no-match return after the loop.

blocks: The first pass establishes global frequencies before any uniqueness decision. The second pass enforces earliest original index. The returned index distinguishes a real unique zero (0,0) from no result (-1,0).

questions.title: Sequential stock requests

body.code: def process_requests(stock, names, amounts, apply=False):

body: Process requests in order. Accept a request only if its item is known and the current available stock is at least the requested amount. An accepted request reduces stock; a rejected one changes nothing. Return (accepted_flags, ending_stock). When apply is False, simulate on a new dictionary and leave stock unchanged. When apply is True, update the supplied stock dictionary itself and return that same dictionary as ending_stock.

stock maps string names to nonnegative integers. names and amounts have equal lengths, 0-1000; amounts are strictly positive integers. Repeated items are allowed. Never create a stock entry for an unknown request. No printing, input, global, dictionary copy/get/items/values, imports, or comprehensions. Copy entries with a loop when simulating.

body.code:
stock = {"bolt": 5, "nut": 2}
process_requests(stock, ["bolt", "bolt", "nut", "pin"], [3, 3, 2, 1])
=> ([True, False, True, False], {"bolt": 2, "nut": 0})
Original stock remains {"bolt": 5, "nut": 2}.

stock = {"bolt": 5}
process_requests(stock, ["bolt", "bolt"], [3, 2], True)
=> ([True, True], {"bolt": 0})
Original stock becomes {"bolt": 0}.

body: Write a top-down plan, include a docstring, and test empty inputs and repeated values. Return results; do not print inside the function.
hints: Choose the working dictionary first: use stock itself for apply=True, or build a new dictionary with for key in stock for simulation.
Check membership before accessing an item. Append one Boolean per request. Only accepted requests subtract stock, and every later request uses the updated working balance.

blocks: Rebinding working = stock intentionally shares the dictionary. The simulation loop copies integer quantities into a distinct dictionary. Repeated requests see earlier accepted withdrawals. A rejected request does not reserve stock. Exact equality is sufficient for acceptance.
Source: L8 dictionary operations; L9 defaults, tuple returns, mutation/rebinding

questions.title: A rectangle and an exponential
body: Evaluate \(\iint_R xe^y\,dA\), where \(R=[0,2]\times[0,\ln3]\). Give an iterated integral in each order.

blocks: \(\int_0^2\int_0^{\ln3}xe^y\,dy\,dx=\int_0^{\ln3}\int_0^2xe^y\,dx\,dy=4\).

questions.title: Average value versus total
body: Let \(f(x,y)=x^2+2y\) on \(R=[-1,1]\times[0,3]\). Find (a) its integral over R and (b) its average value. (c) Find the integral of \(x^3+xy\) over the same region.

questions.title: Midpoints and accuracy
body: Approximate \(\iint_{[0,2]\times[0,2]}(x^2+y^2)\,dA\) using four equal square subrectangles and their midpoints. Then find the exact value and the signed error “approximation minus exact.”

blocks: Midpoint approximation: \(10\). Exact value: \(32/3\). Signed error: \(-2/3\), an underestimate.

questions.title: An order that makes integration possible
body: Reverse the order of \(\int_0^1\int_x^1 e^{y^2}\,dy\,dx\), then evaluate it.

questions.title: A sloping ceiling
body: Find the volume between \(z=x+y\) and \(z=4\) above the triangle \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge0\), \(x+y\le2\). Give a double integral and its value.

questions.title: One region, two descriptions
body: Let D have vertices \((0,0),(2,0),(1,1)\). Write \(\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA\) in each order, splitting if needed. Also find the area of D.

blocks: \(\int_0^1\int_0^x f\,dy\,dx+\int_1^2\int_0^{2-x}f\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1\int_y^{2-y}f\,dx\,dy\). Area: \(1\).

questions.title: Annular accumulation
body: Use polar coordinates to evaluate \(\iint_D(x^2+y^2)\,dA\), where \(1\le x^2+y^2\le4\). Also find the average value of \(x^2+y^2\) on D.

blocks: Integral: \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_1^2r^3\,dr\,d\theta=15\pi/2\). Average: \(5/2\).

questions.title: A disk away from the origin
body: Let \(D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le2x\}\). Give polar bounds and evaluate \(\iint_Dx\,dA\).

blocks: \(-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2\), \(0\le r\le2\cos\theta\). Integral: \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2\cos\theta}r^2\cos\theta\,dr\,d\theta=\pi\).

questions.title: Average distance in a quarter disk
body: Find the average distance from the origin of points in the first-quadrant quarter disk \(x^2+y^2\le4\), using a uniform area average.

questions.title: A nonuniform triangular lamina
body: A plate occupies \(x\ge0,y\ge0,x+y\le2\) and has density \(\delta(x,y)=x\). Find its mass and center of mass.

questions.title: Axis names matter
body: A rectangular plate \(0\le x\le2,0\le y\le1\) has constant density 3. Find its mass, \(I_x\), \(I_y\), and its radius of gyration about the x-axis.

questions.title: Probability on a curved event region
body: Textbook extension: A joint probability density is \(p(x,y)=c(x+y)\) on \([0,1]\times[0,1]\) and zero elsewhere. Find c and \(P(Y\ge X^2)\).

questions.title: Tilted area
body: Find the area of the part of \(z=2x-y+3\) above the triangle \(x\ge0,y\ge0,x+y\le2\).

questions.title: A paraboloid patch
body: Find the curved surface area of \(z=(x^2+y^2)/2\) for \(x^2+y^2\le4\). Do not include a flat cap.

blocks: \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\sqrt{1+r^2}\,r\,dr\,d\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}(5\sqrt5-1)\).

questions.title: Choose a graph carefully
body: Find the curved area of the upper half of the cylinder \(x^2+z^2=4\), between \(y=0\) and \(y=3\). Exclude the end caps. Give the surface-area integral using \(z=f(x,y)\); interpret endpoint singularities as improper limits.

questions.title: A tetrahedron and a weighted total
body: Let \(E=\{x,y,z\ge0:x+y+z\le2\}\). Find (a) its volume, (b) \(\iiint_Ez\,dV\), and (c) its centroid.

questions.title: Reorder nested inequalities
body: The solid E satisfies \(0\le z\le y\le x\le1\). Write its volume integral in the orders \(dz\,dy\,dx\) and \(dx\,dy\,dz\), then evaluate.

blocks: \(\int_0^1\int_0^x\int_0^y1\,dz\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1\int_z^1\int_y^1 1\,dx\,dy\,dz=1/6\).

questions.title: Density changes the balance point
body: A box \(0\le x\le2,0\le y\le1,0\le z\le3\) has volume density \(\delta=z\). Find its mass and center of mass.

questions.title: Paraboloid and plane
body: Use cylindrical coordinates to find the volume above \(z=x^2+y^2\) and below \(z=4\). Include the complete bounds.

questions.title: Resistance to rotation
body: A solid cylinder \(x^2+y^2\le4,0\le z\le3\) has density 1. Find its moment of inertia about the z-axis, using a triple integral.

blocks: \(I_z=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_0^3r^3\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=24\pi\).

questions.title: A sphere with a cylindrical hole
body: Find the volume inside \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le4\) and outside \(x^2+y^2<1\). Give cylindrical bounds and the volume.

blocks: \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_1^2\int_{-\sqrt{4-r^2}}^{\sqrt{4-r^2}}r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=4\pi\sqrt3\).

questions.title: Inside a sphere, above a cone
body: Use spherical coordinates to find the volume inside \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le9\) and above \(z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Phi is measured down from the positive z-axis.

blocks: \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/4}\int_0^3\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=18\pi(1-1/\sqrt2)\).

questions.title: Radial density
body: The ball \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le4\) has density equal to distance from the origin. Find its mass and center of mass.

blocks: \(m=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^2\rho^3\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=16\pi\). Center of mass: \((0,0,0)\).

questions.title: A sphere not centered at the origin
body: Write a spherical-coordinate integral for the volume of \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le2z\), then evaluate. Identify the sphere's center and radius.

blocks: \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2\cos\phi}\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=4\pi/3\). Center \((0,0,1)\), radius \(1\).

questions.title: Straighten a parallelogram
body: Let D be defined by \(0\le x+y\le2\) and \(0\le x-y\le1\). Use \(u=x+y,v=x-y\) to evaluate \(\iint_D(x^2-y^2)\,dA\). State the absolute Jacobian.

blocks: \(|\partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v)|=1/2\). Integral: \(\int_0^2\int_0^1\frac{uv}{2}\,dv\,du=1/2\).

questions.title: Scale an ellipse
body: For \(D=\{x^2/9+y^2/4\le1\}\), use \(x=3r\cos\theta,y=2r\sin\theta\) to evaluate \(\iint_D(x^2/9+y^2/4)\,dA\). Give the transformed area element.

blocks: \(dA=6r\,dr\,d\theta\). Integral: \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 6r^3\,dr\,d\theta=3\pi\).

questions.title: Scale an ellipsoid
body: Let \(E=\{x^2/4+y^2/9+z^2/16\le1\}\). Use \(x=2u,y=3v,z=4w\) to find (a) its volume and (b) the average value of \(x^2\) on E. State the absolute Jacobian.

blocks: Absolute Jacobian: \(24\). (a) \(32\pi\). (b) \(4/5\).

questions.title: Read a curved region in both orders
body: Let D lie between \(y=x^2\) and \(y=x\) in the first quadrant. Use the diagram to write both orders of integration and evaluate \(\iint_D(x+y)\,dA\).
questions.figureAlt: xy projection. x; y; y = x; y = x²

blocks: The intersections are \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\). Vertical slices give \(0\le x\le1,\ x^2\le y\le x\); horizontal slices give \(0\le y\le1,\ y\le x\le\sqrt y\).
\(\int_0^1\int_{x^2}^x(x+y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1\int_y^{\sqrt y}(x+y)\,dx\,dy=3/20\).

questions.title: Polar coordinates on a shifted disk
body: D is the disk \((x-1)^2+y^2\le1\). Evaluate \(\iint_D(x^2+y^2)\,dA\) in polar coordinates.
questions.figureAlt: xy projection (upper half; reflect across x-axis). x; y; (x − 1)² + y² = 1; 1; 2

blocks: The circle becomes \(r=2\cos\theta\), so \(-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2\) and \(0\le r\le2\cos\theta\). Remember \(dA=r\,dr\,d\theta\).
\(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2\cos\theta}r^3\,dr\,d\theta=4\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^4\theta\,d\theta=3\pi/2\).

questions.title: A triangular lamina with variable density
body: A lamina occupies \(x\ge0,y\ge0,x+y\le2\) with density \(\delta=x+y\). Find its mass and center of mass.
questions.figureAlt: xy projection. x; y; x + y = 2

blocks: \(m=\int_0^2\int_0^{2-x}(x+y)\,dy\,dx=8/3\). Symmetry about \(y=x\) gives \(\bar x=\bar y\).

questions.title: Surface area of a paraboloid cap
body: Find the area of \(z=x^2+y^2\) above the disk \(x^2+y^2\le1\). Explain why this is not the volume under the surface.
questions.figureAlt: rz cross-section (rotate about z-axis). r; z; z = r²; 1

blocks: \(f_x=2x,f_y=2y\), so the surface element is \(\sqrt{1+4x^2+4y^2}\,dA\).
\(A=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1r\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,dr\,d\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}(5\sqrt5-1)\). The integrand measures stretched surface area; volume would use height \(r^2\).

questions.title: Challenge: weighted tetrahedron
body: E is bounded by the coordinate planes and \(x+2y+3z=6\). With density \(\delta=z\), find the mass and \(\bar z\).
questions.figureAlt: xz cross-section at y = 0. x; z; x + 3z = 6

blocks: Bounds: \(0\le z\le2,\ 0\le y\le(6-3z)/2,\ 0\le x\le6-2y-3z\). A horizontal slice has area \(A(z)=(6-3z)^2/4\).

questions.title: Challenge: put z on the outside
body: The solid is \(0\le y\le x\le1,\ 0\le z\le y^2\). Rewrite its volume integral in the order \(dx\,dy\,dz\) and evaluate.
questions.figureAlt: yz projection. y; z; z = y²; 1

blocks: The yz projection satisfies \(0\le z\le1,\ \sqrt z\le y\le1\). For each point in that projection, \(y\le x\le1\).
\(V=\int_0^1\int_{\sqrt z}^1\int_y^1 1\,dx\,dy\,dz=1/12\). Check in the original order: \(\int_0^1 y^2(1-y)\,dy=1/12\).

questions.title: Challenge: inertia between two paraboloids
body: E lies between \(z=x^2+y^2\) and \(z=8-x^2-y^2\). For constant density 1, find the volume and moment of inertia \(I_z=\iiint_E(x^2+y^2)\,dV\).
questions.figureAlt: rz cross-section (rotate about z-axis). r; z; z = 8 − r²; z = r²; (2, 4)

blocks: The surfaces meet at \(r=2,z=4\). Bounds: \(0\le\theta\le2\pi,0\le r\le2,r^2\le z\le8-r^2\).
\(I_z=2\pi\int_0^2(8-2r^2)r^3\,dr=64\pi/3\). The extra \(r^2\) is squared distance to the z-axis.

questions.title: Challenge: an offset cylinder with density
body: E satisfies \((x-1)^2+y^2\le1\) and \(0\le z\le x^2+y^2\). Find its mass for density \(\delta=z\).
questions.figureAlt: xy projection (upper half; reflect across x-axis). x; y; r = 2 cos θ

blocks: The offset cylinder gives \(-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2,\ 0\le r\le2\cos\theta\). The height is \(0\le z\le r^2\).
\(m=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2\cos\theta}\int_0^{r^2}zr\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=\frac{16}{3}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^6\theta\,d\theta=5\pi/3\).

questions.title: Challenge: spherical shell inside a cone
body: E lies between spheres \(\rho=1\) and \(\rho=3\), above the cone \(z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}/\sqrt3\). Find its mass if \(\delta=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\).
questions.figureAlt: rz cross-section (rotate about z-axis). r; z; ρ = 3; ρ = 1; φ = π/3

blocks: The cone is \(\phi=\pi/3\). Above it means \(0\le\phi\le\pi/3\). Density is \(\rho\), and \(dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\).
\(m=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/3}\int_1^3\rho^3\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=20\pi\).

questions.title: Challenge: inside one sphere, outside another
body: Find the volume inside \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le2z\) and outside \(x^2+y^2+z^2\ge1\). Determine where the radial bounds meet.
questions.figureAlt: rz cross-section (rotate about z-axis). r; z; ρ = 2 cos φ; ρ = 1

blocks: The shifted sphere is \(\rho=2\cos\phi\). Since \(1\le\rho\le2\cos\phi\), the bounds meet at \(\phi=\pi/3\).
\(V=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/3}\int_1^{2\cos\phi}\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=11\pi/12\). Integrating to \(\pi/2\) would reverse radial bounds in part of the region.

questions.title: Challenge: a cylindrical hole through a sphere
body: A sphere \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le4\) has the cylindrical region \(x^2+y^2<1\) removed. Find the remaining volume using cylindrical coordinates.
questions.figureAlt: rz cross-section (upper half; reflect across r-axis). r; z; 1; r² + z² = 4

blocks: The remaining solid has \(1\le r\le2\) and \(-\sqrt{4-r^2}\le z\le\sqrt{4-r^2}\). Use symmetry across the xy-plane.
\(V=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_1^2\int_{-\sqrt{4-r^2}}^{\sqrt{4-r^2}}r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=4\pi\int_1^2r\sqrt{4-r^2}\,dr=4\pi\sqrt3\).

questions.title: Challenge: ellipsoid moment of inertia
body: For the uniform solid \(x^2/4+y^2/9+z^2/16\le1\) with density 1, use a change of variables to compute \(I_z=\iiint_E(x^2+y^2)\,dV\).
questions.figureAlt: xz cross-section at y = 0 (upper half). x; z; x²/4 + z²/16 = 1

blocks: Set \(x=2u,y=3v,z=4w\). The transformed region is the unit ball B and the absolute Jacobian is \(24\).
\(I_z=24\iiint_B(4u^2+9v^2)\,dV\). By symmetry each of \(\iiint_Bu^2\,dV,\iiint_Bv^2\,dV,\iiint_Bw^2\,dV\) equals \(4\pi/15\).
Therefore \(I_z=24(13)(4\pi/15)=416\pi/5\). The mass is \(32\pi\), giving the check \(I_z=m(2^2+3^2)/5\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: overlapping disks with a radial weight
body: Let D be the intersection of \(x^2+y^2\le2x\) and \(x^2+y^2\le2y\). Use polar coordinates to evaluate \(\iint_D(x^2+y^2)\,dA\). Explain where the radial bound changes.

blocks: Both inequalities require \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\), and \(r\le\min(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta)\). The bounds switch at \(\theta=\pi/4\).
Reflection across \(y=x\) makes the two terms equal.

questions.title: Harder challenge: a cardioid with a circular cutout
body: Find the area inside the cardioid \(r=1+\cos\theta\) and outside the circle \(r=1\). Determine the angular interval before integrating.

blocks: The radial interval \(1\le r\le1+\cos\theta\) is nonempty only when \(\cos\theta\ge0\). Use \(-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: an improper Gaussian sector
body: Evaluate \(\iint_D(x^2+y^2)e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dA\), where D is the unbounded sector \(x\ge0,\ 0\le y\le\sqrt3x\). Write the improper limit explicitly.

blocks: The sector is \(0\le\theta\le\pi/3,\ 0\le r<\infty\). The radial weight and Jacobian together give \(r^3\).
Use \(u=r^2\) and integration by parts. The limit is finite, so the improper integral converges.

questions.title: Harder challenge: balance and inertia of a curved lamina
body: A lamina occupies \(0\le x\le1,\ x^2\le y\le x\), with density \(\delta=x\). Find its mass, center of mass, and polar moment of inertia about the origin \(I_O=\iint_D(x^2+y^2)\delta\,dA\).

blocks: Divide the first moments by mass: \((\bar x,\bar y)=(3/5,1/2)\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: a radially weighted quarter annulus
body: A lamina occupies \(1\le x^2+y^2\le9\) in the first quadrant and has density \(\delta=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Find its mass, center of mass, and polar moment \(I_O\).

blocks: Use \(1\le r\le3,\ 0\le\theta\le\pi/2\). Density contributes one factor of r and the area element contributes another.

questions.title: Harder challenge: a normalized density on a triangle
body: A joint probability density is \(p(x,y)=cxy\) on \(x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ x+y\le1\), and zero elsewhere. Find c and \(P(Y\ge2X)\).

blocks: The event has \(2x\le y\le1-x\), which requires \(0\le x\le1/3\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: a cubic radial surface
body: Find the curved area of \(z=\frac23(x^2+y^2)^{3/2}\) above the unit disk. Give an exact answer using a logarithm.

questions.title: Harder challenge: a spherical patch over an annular sector
body: Find the area of the upper sphere \(z=\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}\) above \(1\le x^2+y^2\le4,\ y\ge x\ge0\). Exclude all planar faces.

blocks: The surface factor is \(\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2}=3/\sqrt{9-r^2}\). The projection has \(1\le r\le2\) and \(\pi/4\le\theta\le\pi/2\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: total boundary area of a truncated solid
body: Let E be the solid \(1\le z\le4,\ x^2+y^2\le z\). Find its total boundary area, including both flat faces. Identify the projection of the curved face.

blocks: The curved face is \(z=x^2+y^2\) over the annulus \(1\le r\le2\); it is not the full disk. Its surface factor is \(\sqrt{1+4r^2}\).
The bottom disk at z=1 has area \(\pi\), and the top disk at z=4 has area \(4\pi\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: density on an asymmetric tetrahedron
body: The solid \(E=\{x,y,z\ge0:x+y+z\le1\}\) has density \(\delta=xy\). Find its mass and all three coordinates of its center of mass.

blocks: Symmetry gives equal x- and y-moments, but z is not interchangeable with them because the density is xy.

questions.title: Harder challenge: a sloping roof with z outermost
body: Let \(E=\{0\le x\le1,\ 0\le y\le1,\ 0\le z\le x+y\}\). Rewrite \(\iiint_E z^2\,dV\) in the order \(dx\,dy\,dz\), splitting as needed, and evaluate.

blocks: For fixed z, the square is clipped by \(x+y\ge z\). For \(0\le z\le1\), split at y=z; for \(1\le z\le2\), y starts at z−1.
Check in the original order: \(\int_0^1\int_0^1 (x+y)^3/3\,dy\,dx=1/2\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: mass between two sloping planes
body: Let \(E=\{x,y\ge0,\ x+y\le1,\ x+y\le z\le2-x-y\}\), with density \(\delta=z\). Find the mass and \(\bar z\).

blocks: Integrate in z first. Writing s=x+y only as an abbreviation, the mass integrand becomes \(((2-s)^2-s^2)/2=2-2s\).
The geometric solid is symmetric about z=1, but the density increases with z, shifting the balance point above that plane.

questions.title: Harder challenge: a cone with vertical density
body: A solid lies above \(z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and below \(z=2\), with density \(\delta=z\). Find its mass, \(\bar z\), and moment of inertia \(I_z\) about the z-axis.

blocks: Use \(0\le\theta\le2\pi,\ 0\le r\le2,\ r\le z\le2\).
For inertia, multiply density by squared distance \(r^2\) before including the Jacobian r.

questions.title: Harder challenge: competing lower surfaces
body: A uniform solid of density 1 lies above both \(z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and \(z=x^2+y^2\), and below \(z=2\). Find its volume and \(\bar z\). Explain the necessary radial split.

blocks: The lower surface is \(\max(r,r^2)\): r for \(0\le r\le1\) and \(r^2\) for \(1\le r\le\sqrt2\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: an offset cylinder under a plane
body: Let E satisfy \(x^2+y^2\le2x\) and \(0\le z\le x\). For density 1, find its volume and centroid using cylindrical coordinates.

blocks: Bounds are \(-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2,\ 0\le r\le2\cos\theta,\ 0\le z\le r\cos\theta\). Reflection in y=0 gives \(\bar y=0\).
Integrating z first gives \(\iiint_E z\,dV=\frac12\iint_Dx^2\,dA=5\pi/8\). Thus \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)=(5/4,0,5/8)\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: radial density in a spherical cap
body: The solid \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le4,\ z\ge1\) has density \(\delta=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\). Find its mass using spherical coordinates, with \(\phi\) measured from the positive z-axis.

blocks: The plane gives \(\rho\cos\phi\ge1\), so \(\sec\phi\le\rho\le2\). These bounds are compatible for \(0\le\phi\le\pi/3\).
With \(u=\cos\phi\), the remaining integral is \(\int_{1/2}^1(16-u^{-4})\,du=17/3\). Thus \(m=17\pi/6\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: a shifted sphere clipped by a cone
body: A uniform solid of density 1 lies inside \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le4z\) and above \(z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Find its volume and centroid using spherical coordinates.

blocks: The sphere becomes \(\rho=4\cos\phi\); the cone restricts \(0\le\phi\le\pi/4\). Use \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\) and \(0\le\rho\le4\cos\phi\). Rotational symmetry gives \(\bar x=\bar y=0\).

questions.title: Harder challenge: weighted hemispherical shell
body: The upper hemispherical shell \(1\le x^2+y^2+z^2\le4,\ z\ge0\) has density \(\delta=x^2+y^2+z^2\). Find its mass, center of mass, and moment of inertia about the z-axis.

blocks: Use \(1\le\rho\le2,\ 0\le\phi\le\pi/2,\ 0\le\theta\le2\pi\), and density \(\rho^2\).
Squared distance to the z-axis is \(\rho^2\sin^2\phi\), not \(\rho^2\).

questions.title: Threshold wavelength from binding energy
body: A metal has work function 4.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Which pair correctly gives its threshold wavelength and whether 500 nm light can eject electrons?

blocks: B. 473 nm; no
Why: λ₀ = hc/φ = 473 nm; 500 nm photons have less energy than the work function.

questions.title: Maximum photoelectron energy
body: A metal has work function 3.10 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and is illuminated at 400.0 nm. What is the maximum electron kinetic energy?

blocks: Why: The photon supplies 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; subtract the work function.

questions.title: Brightness versus photon energy
body: A surface ejects electrons under 450 nm light but not under 650 nm light. In the ordinary single-photon model, select every statement that must be true.
choices: At fixed 450 nm wavelength, higher intensity supplies more photons per second to the same area.
The work function is greater than a 650 nm photon’s energy and no greater than a 450 nm photon’s energy.
670 nm photons must eject electrons if the beam is bright enough.
Doubling 450 nm intensity increases maximum electron kinetic energy.

blocks: A, B, C. At fixed 450 nm wavelength, higher intensity supplies more photons per second to the same area. | The work function is greater than a 650 nm photon’s energy and no greater than a 450 nm photon’s energy. | 400 nm photons can eject electrons.
Why: Threshold depends on energy per photon; intensity changes photon arrival rate, not hc/λ.

questions.title: Shortest emitted wavelength
body: Which listed H transition emits the shortest-wavelength photon?

blocks: Why: Emission is downward; the largest energy drop gives the shortest wavelength.

questions.title: Read an energy-level diagram
body: The diagram labels four transitions. Select every true statement.
choices: B and C emit photons of equal energy.
For B, the atom’s ΔE is negative while photon energy is positive.
B emits a shorter wavelength than C.

blocks: C, D, E. For B, the atom’s ΔE is negative while photon energy is positive. | A is absorption. | B emits a shorter wavelength than C.
Why: A rises from 1 to 3; B is 3 → 1, C is 3 → 2, and D rises 2 → 4. Compare energy gaps, not arrow lengths on an arbitrary drawing.

questions.figureAlt: Hydrogen levels n=1 to 4. A:1→3, B:3→1, C:3→2, D:2→4.

questions.title: Find the emitted wavelength
body: An H electron falls from n = 4 to n = 2. Which pair gives the emitted wavelength and sign of ΔEatom?

blocks: D. 486 nm; negative

questions.title: Choose the invalid quantum-number tuple
body: Which tuple (n, ℓ, mℓ, mₛ) is NOT allowed?

blocks: Why: For n = 3, ℓ can only be 0, 1, or 2.

questions.title: Several tuples can be invalid
body: Select every INVALID tuple (n, ℓ, mℓ, mₛ).

blocks: Why: mℓ must lie from −ℓ to +ℓ, spin is ±½, and ℓ must be less than n.

questions.title: Invalid versus merely unoccupied
body: For a ground-state Ne atom, which description is correct? Ne has configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶.
choices: (3,2,0,+½) is allowed but unoccupied; (2,2,0,+½) is forbidden.
Both tuples are forbidden because Ne has no n=3 electrons.
Both tuples are occupied because d can hold 10 electrons.
(3,2,0,+½) is forbidden; (2,2,0,+½) is allowed but unoccupied.

blocks: A. (3,2,0,+½) is allowed but unoccupied; (2,2,0,+½) is forbidden.
Why: Quantum-number validity is independent of the electron population in the chosen atom.

questions.title: Count actual electrons with a specified mℓ
body: A ground-state Kr atom has [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶. How many of its electrons have mℓ = +1?

blocks: Why: Filled 2p, 3p, 3d, and 4p each contain two electrons with mℓ = +1.

questions.title: Leave some quantum numbers unspecified
body: What is the maximum number of electrons in one atom with n = 4 and mℓ = 0?

blocks: Why: There is one mℓ = 0 orbital in each of 4s, 4p, 4d, and 4f; each holds two electrons.

questions.title: Capacity and population are different
body: Select every correct statement about allowed electron capacities and ground-state Ar, 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶.
choices: The n = 3 shell can hold at most 18 electrons.
The specified set n=3, ℓ=1, mℓ=0, mₛ=+½ can describe at most 2 electrons in one atom.
Every ground-state Ar electron with n=3 has ℓ=1.
Exactly 4 electrons in ground-state Ar have mℓ = +1.
The 3d subshell is allowed but empty in ground-state Ar.

blocks: A, D, E. The n = 3 shell can hold at most 18 electrons. | Exactly 4 electrons in ground-state Ar have mℓ = +1. | The 3d subshell is allowed but empty in ground-state Ar.
Why: A full shell has capacity 2n²; actual Ar occupies 3s and 3p but not 3d. Four specified quantum numbers identify at most one electron.

questions.title: Rank an isoelectronic series
body: Which order is increasing ionic radius? Z: O=8, F=9, Na=11, Mg=12.

blocks: C. Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < F⁻ < O²⁻
Why: All contain 10 electrons; greater nuclear charge gives a smaller ion.

questions.title: Combine ion and atom radius comparisons
body: Select every correct radius comparison using the standard main-group/isolated-ion trends.
choices: Mg²⁺ is larger than Ca²⁺ because it has fewer electrons.
S²⁻ is smaller than Cl⁻ in their isoelectronic series.

blocks: A, B, E. Cl⁻ is larger than Cl. | Fe³⁺ is smaller than Fe²⁺. | K is larger than Ca.
Why: Cation charge, anion expansion, period trends, and isoelectronic nuclear attraction must be applied to the appropriate pairs.

questions.title: Size is not set by charge alone
body: Which comparison and reason are both correct?
choices: O²⁻ < F⁻ because O²⁻ has the more negative charge.
Ca²⁺ > K⁺ because Ca has the higher atomic number.
Rb⁺ > K⁺ because Rb⁺ has its outer occupied electrons in a larger principal shell.
Rb⁺ < K⁺ because all ions with more protons must be smaller.

blocks: C. Rb⁺ > K⁺ because Rb⁺ has its outer occupied electrons in a larger principal shell.
Why: Rb⁺ and K⁺ are not isoelectronic with each other; compare their occupied shells first.

questions.title: Infer an element from an ionization jump
body: A period-3 element has IE₁=578, IE₂=1817, IE₃=2745, IE₄=11,577 kJ/mol. Which element and usual simple-ion charge fit?

blocks: C. Al; +3
Why: The large jump after three removals indicates three valence electrons; period 3 gives Al.

questions.title: Locate the core-electron jump
body: For a ground-state phosphorus atom, [Ne]3s²3p³, the largest initial valence-to-core jump occurs between which successive ionization energies?

blocks: C. IE₅ and IE₆
Why: Five valence electrons are removed before the first n=2 core electron.

questions.title: Exceptions to a simple left-to-right arrow
body: Select every correct first-ionization-energy comparison or explanation.
choices: IE₁(Be) > IE₁(B): B loses a higher-energy 2p electron.
IE₁ is normally negative because removing electrons releases energy.
IE₁(N) > IE₁(O): pairing in O’s 2p orbitals makes removal easier.
IE₁(Mg) < IE₁(Al) because the trend has no exceptions.
Successive ionization energies generally increase for a given element.

blocks: A, C, E. IE₁(Be) > IE₁(B): B loses a higher-energy 2p electron. | IE₁(N) > IE₁(O): pairing in O’s 2p orbitals makes removal easier. | Successive ionization energies generally increase for a given element.
Why: Subshell energy and pairing explain the familiar Be/B and N/O exceptions; removing a bound electron costs energy.

questions.title: Paramagnetism of an ion
body: Which isolated ground-state ion is paramagnetic? Use Hund’s rule for the d orbitals. Z: Ca=20, Ti=22, Fe=26, Zn=30.

blocks: C. Fe³⁺
Why: Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵ with five unpaired electrons; the others have closed-shell configurations.

questions.title: Count unpaired d electrons
body: For isolated Co²⁺ (Z=27), which pair correctly gives its condensed configuration and number of unpaired electrons? Assume Hund’s-rule d occupancy.

blocks: A. [Ar]3d⁷; 3
Why: Remove the 4s electrons first, then fill the five degenerate d orbitals by Hund’s rule.

questions.title: Read orbital diagrams
body: The three panels show proposed p⁴ arrangements. Select every correct statement.
choices: Panel B violates the Pauli exclusion principle.
Panel B has all electrons paired but is not the Hund’s-rule ground-state arrangement.
Panel C is forbidden by Pauli exclusion.
Panel A is the Hund’s-rule ground-state arrangement and has 2 unpaired electrons.
An even total electron count always means diamagnetism.

blocks: B, C, D. Panel B has all electrons paired but is not the Hund’s-rule ground-state arrangement. | Panel C is forbidden by Pauli exclusion. | Panel A is the Hund’s-rule ground-state arrangement and has 2 unpaired electrons.
Why: A is [↑↓][↑][↑]; B is prematurely paired; C puts parallel spins into the same orbital.

questions.figureAlt: Three p4 orbital diagrams: A [↑↓][↑][↑], B [↑↓][↑↓][ ], C [↑↑][↑][↑].

questions.title: Find the pair with different configurations
body: Which pair does NOT have identical isolated ground-state electron configurations? Z: Cr=24, Fe=26, Cu=29, Zn=30.

blocks: B. Cr and Fe²⁺
Why: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹, whereas Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶. Equal electron count is not enough for all open-shell transition-metal comparisons.

questions.title: Configuration exceptions survive careful electron removal
body: Which set is correct? Z(Cu)=29.

blocks: A. Cu [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹; Cu⁺ [Ar]3d¹⁰; Cu²⁺ [Ar]3d⁹
Why: Neutral Cu is an Aufbau-pattern exception; its highest-n 4s electron is lost before 3d electrons.

questions.title: Choose identical electron configurations
body: Select every pair with identical ground-state configurations. Atomic numbers: Ar18, K19, Ca20, Cr24, Fe26, Cu29, Zn30.

blocks: A, C, E. K⁺ and Ca²⁺ | Ar and S²⁻ | Cu⁺ and Zn²⁺
Why: The first and fourth pairs are [Ar]; Cu⁺ and Zn²⁺ are [Ar]3d¹⁰. Cr versus Fe²⁺ is the important same-electron-count exception.

questions.title: Choose a valid carbonyl Lewis structure
body: The diagram shows four proposed Lewis structures for COCl₂. Which panel satisfies electron count, second-period octets, and the usual lowest-formal-charge preference? Valence electrons: C4, O6, Cl7.

blocks: A. Panel A
Why: A uses 24 electrons, gives every atom an octet, and has zero formal charges. B overfills C; C leaves C short of an octet; D overfills O.

questions.figureAlt: COCl2 candidates with all lone pairs shown. A has C=O and two C-Cl; B also has a C=Cl; C has only single bonds; D has C=O but an extra O lone pair.

questions.title: Choose an octet structure for an ion
body: Which description is the best major Lewis contributor for NO₂⁻? N5, O6 valence electrons.
choices: Two N=O bonds and one lone pair on N.
One N=O, one N–O, one lone pair on N; double O has two lone pairs and single O three.
Two N–O bonds, no lone pair on N, and three lone pairs on each O.
One N=O and one N–O, but no lone pair on N.

blocks: B. One N=O, one N–O, one lone pair on N; double O has two lone pairs and single O three.
Why: 18 total electrons give N one lone pair and an octet with one double and one single bond; the other equivalent form swaps O positions.

questions.title: An incomplete octet can be correct
body: Which is the preferred introductory Lewis description for an isolated BF₃ molecule? B3 and F7 valence electrons.
choices: Three B–F single bonds; no B lone pair; three lone pairs on each F; B has six surrounding electrons.
Three B=F bonds give B an ordinary allowed second-period expanded octet.
Three B–F single bonds and one B lone pair; the neutral molecule has 26 electrons.
One B=F double bond and two B–F single bonds are required because B can never have fewer than eight electrons.

blocks: A. Three B–F single bonds; no B lone pair; three lone pairs on each F; B has six surrounding electrons.
Why: BF₃ is a common electron-deficient exception: 24 total electrons, six around B, with zero formal charges in the single-bond drawing.

questions.title: Infer net charge from every electron pair
body: The drawing shows N=C=O with two lone pairs on N, two on O, and none on C. What is its formula including net charge? N5, C4, O6 valence electrons.
questions.familyTitle: Infer a formula or charge from a drawing

blocks: D. NCO⁻
Why: The drawing contains 16 electrons; the neutral valence sum is 15, so its charge is −1.

questions.figureAlt: N=C=O with two lone pairs on each terminal atom; no central lone pair.

questions.title: A second drawing, a different charge
body: The diagram shows a C center with three O neighbors: one double bond and two single bonds. Double O has two lone pairs; each single O has three. No lone pairs are on C. What species is shown?
questions.familyTitle: Infer a formula or charge from a drawing

blocks: D. CO₃²⁻
Why: The 24 drawn electrons exceed the neutral C+3O sum of 22 by two.

questions.figureAlt: Carbon connected to three oxygens, one double and two single; all terminal lone pairs shown.

questions.title: Check a drawing by two independent methods
body: The same N=C=O drawing has two lone pairs on N and on O. Select every true statement. N5, C4, O6 valence electrons.
choices: The N and O atoms each have an octet.
Its net charge is +1 because N is less electronegative than O.
The formal charges on N, C, O are −1, 0, 0.
questions.familyTitle: Infer a formula or charge from a drawing

blocks: A, B, C, E. The net charge is −1. | The drawing contains 16 valence electrons. | The N and O atoms each have an octet. | The formal charges on N, C, O are −1, 0, 0.
Why: Electron excess and the sum of formal charges independently give charge −1; all three atoms have octets.

questions.figureAlt: N=C=O with two lone pairs on each terminal atom.

questions.title: Formal charge versus oxidation state
body: In a major NO₃⁻ contributor, N has one double bond and two single bonds and no lone pairs. What are N’s formal charge and oxidation number? Take O oxidation number as −2.

blocks: C. FC +1; oxidation number +5
Why: FC = 5 − 4 = +1; charge balance x + 3(−2) = −1 gives oxidation number +5.

questions.title: Assign formal charges from a labeled structure
body: For the depicted O₃ contributor, the terminal double-bonded O has two lone pairs, central O one, and terminal single-bonded O three. What are the formal charges in that order?

blocks: Why: For oxygen, FC = 6 − nonbonding electrons − sum of bond orders.

questions.figureAlt: O=O–O with terminal double O two lone pairs, central O one lone pair, single O three lone pairs.

questions.title: Oxidation-number exceptions and formal charge
body: Select every correct statement.
choices: In H₂O₂, H is +1 and O is −1.
In OF₂, oxygen is −2 because oxygen has no exceptions.
A carbon oxidation number of +4 in CO₂ proves that it contains isolated C⁴⁺ ions.
Formal charges sum to the overall species charge.
In NaH, Na is +1 and H is −1.

blocks: A, D, E. In H₂O₂, H is +1 and O is −1. | Formal charges sum to the overall species charge. | In NaH, Na is +1 and H is −1.
Why: Peroxides and metal hydrides are exceptions; F forces O to +2 in OF₂. Formal charge and oxidation state are bookkeeping conventions.

questions.title: Equivalent nitrate contributors
body: How many equivalent major octet resonance contributors does NO₃⁻ have, and what is its average N–O bond order?

blocks: Why: One N=O can be placed at any of three equivalent oxygen sites; (2+1+1)/3 = 4/3.

questions.title: Nitrite versus nitrate
body: Which comparison is correct? Use equivalent major octet contributors.
choices: NO₂⁻ has 2 contributors and average order 1.5; NO₃⁻ has 3 and average order 4/3.
NO₃⁻ alternates between one short and two long bonds at every instant.
NO₂⁻ has 1 contributor because its O atoms are permanently different.
Both have 3 contributors and average order 4/3.

blocks: A. NO₂⁻ has 2 contributors and average order 1.5; NO₃⁻ has 3 and average order 4/3.
Why: Equivalent oxygen positions produce delocalized real bonds; the hybrid is not a sequence of switching Lewis structures.

questions.title: What resonance does and does not mean
body: Select every true statement.
choices: Atoms retain the same connectivity in resonance forms.
All possible resonance contributors necessarily have equal weights.
A C–O order of 4/3 is an average bonding description, not 4/3 of a localized two-electron pair fixed in one bond.
Equivalent contributors to CO₃²⁻ give equal C–O bond lengths in the actual ion.
A resonance arrow means that the molecule rapidly changes into different compounds.

blocks: A, C, D. Atoms retain the same connectivity in resonance forms. | A C–O order of 4/3 is an average bonding description, not 4/3 of a localized two-electron pair fixed in one bond. | Equivalent contributors to CO₃²⁻ give equal C–O bond lengths in the actual ion.
Why: Electron placement varies between contributors; nuclei/connectivity do not. Unequal contributors should not be averaged with equal weights.

questions.title: Shape from a supplied Lewis pattern
body: In ClO₃F, a supplied Lewis contributor has Cl bonded to three O atoms by double bonds and to F by a single bond, with no Cl lone pair. What is the molecular geometry at Cl?

blocks: D. Tetrahedral
Why: Four neighboring atoms give four domains; multiple bonds each count once. Four bonds and no lone pairs give AX₄.

questions.title: Five domains, four bonded atoms
body: SF₄ has 34 valence electrons. After S–F bonds and F octets are filled, one lone pair remains on S. What are its electron geometry and molecular shape?

blocks: B. Trigonal bipyramidal; seesaw
Why: Four bonds plus one lone pair give five domains; the lone pair is equatorial.

questions.title: Lone-pair variants of six domains
body: Select every correct geometry assignment.
choices: XeF₄: octahedral electron geometry, square-planar molecular shape.
SF₆: octahedral electron and molecular geometries.
BrF₅: octahedral electron geometry, square-pyramidal molecular shape.
ClF₃: trigonal-bipyramidal electron geometry, T-shaped molecular shape.
XeF₂: tetrahedral electron geometry, bent molecular shape.

blocks: A, B, C, D. XeF₄: octahedral electron geometry, square-planar molecular shape. | SF₆: octahedral electron and molecular geometries. | BrF₅: octahedral electron geometry, square-pyramidal molecular shape. | ClF₃: trigonal-bipyramidal electron geometry, T-shaped molecular shape.
Why: Count central lone pairs as well as bonds: XeF₂ has five domains and is linear, not bent.

questions.title: A two-bond anion need not be linear
body: PH₂⁻ has P as the center. P has 5 and H 1 valence electron. Which prediction follows the lecture VSEPR model?

blocks: C. Bent; H–P–H <109.5°
Why: 5+2+1=8 electrons; two bonds leave two lone pairs on P. AX₂E₂ has tetrahedral electron geometry and a bent shape.

questions.title: A double bond distorts a planar center
body: For O=CCl₂ with no central lone pair, which angle comparison is predicted by simple VSEPR?

blocks: B. Cl–C–Cl <120° and O–C–Cl >120°
Why: The double-bond domain repels adjacent single-bond domains more strongly and compresses the angle between those single bonds.

questions.title: Angle reasoning across familiar molecules
body: Select every statement consistent with the introductory VSEPR model.
choices: All sp³ centers must have an experimental angle of exactly 109.5°.
CH₄ has ideal H–C–H angles of 109.5°.
The two bonds in CO₂ count as four domains because they are double bonds.
Lone pairs prefer equatorial positions in a trigonal-bipyramidal arrangement.
NH₃ and H₂O have tetrahedral electron geometry but smaller bond angles than CH₄.

blocks: B, D, E. CH₄ has ideal H–C–H angles of 109.5°. | Lone pairs prefer equatorial positions in a trigonal-bipyramidal arrangement. | NH₃ and H₂O have tetrahedral electron geometry but smaller bond angles than CH₄.
Why: Domain geometry gives ideal angles; lone pairs and unequal bonding domains produce distortions.

questions.title: Hybridization of a charged central atom
body: For SnCl₃⁻, use Sn4 and Cl7 valence electrons and the lecture localized model. Which description is correct at Sn?
choices: sp³; one lone pair; trigonal pyramidal
sp²; zero lone pairs; trigonal planar

blocks: A. sp³; one lone pair; trigonal pyramidal
Why: 4+21+1=26 electrons. Three bonds and Cl octets leave one Sn lone pair: four domains.

questions.title: Four bonds can require six hybrid directions
body: Which pair of lecture-model hybridizations is correct for PCl₄⁺ and XeF₄? P5, Cl7, Xe8, F7 valence electrons.
choices: Both sp³ because each has four bonded atoms

blocks: B. PCl₄⁺ sp³; XeF₄ sp³d²
Why: PCl₄⁺ has four bonds/no lone pair; XeF₄ has four bonds/two lone pairs. The d-containing label is the course’s simplified model.

questions.title: Hybridization bookkeeping for ions
body: Select every correct lecture-model assignment.
choices: BF₄⁻: B is sp² because neutral BF₃ is sp².

blocks: A, B, C, E. NO₂⁻: N is sp². | ClF₃: Cl is sp³d. | NH₄⁺: N is sp³. | I₃⁻: central I is sp³d.
Why: Use the actual charged species: BF₄⁻ has four domains, so it is sp³. I₃⁻ and ClF₃ each have five domains.

questions.title: Read a labeled carbon in a structure
body: In the labeled molecule, which hybridization describes C5? Use the localized lecture model.

blocks: A. sp
Why: The nitrile carbon has two neighbors and two σ-domain directions despite its triple bond.

questions.figureAlt: CH₂(C1)=CH(C2)–C3(=O)–CH₂(C4)–C5≡N, with all carbon labels visible.

questions.title: Read two different local environments
body: For the same labeled molecule, what are the hybridizations of C3 and C4, respectively?

blocks: D. sp²; sp³
Why: The carbonyl carbon has three domains; the methylene carbon has four.

questions.figureAlt: CH₂(C1)=CH(C2)–C3(=O)–CH₂(C4)–C5≡N.

questions.title: Hybrid orbitals versus p orbitals
body: For the labeled molecule, select every true statement in the localized model.
choices: C4 is sp³ and contributes no unhybridized valence p orbital to a localized π bond.
The π part of C1=C2 forms through end-to-end overlap of sp² hybrids.
C5 retains two unhybridized p orbitals for π bonding.
C1 retains one unhybridized p orbital for π bonding.
The C3–C4 σ bond can be described as sp²–sp³ overlap.

blocks: A, C, D, E. C4 is sp³ and contributes no unhybridized valence p orbital to a localized π bond. | C5 retains two unhybridized p orbitals for π bonding. | C1 retains one unhybridized p orbital for π bonding. | The C3–C4 σ bond can be described as sp²–sp³ overlap.
Why: Hybrids describe the σ framework; parallel unhybridized p orbitals supply π overlap.

questions.figureAlt: CH₂(C1)=CH(C2)–C3(=O)–CH₂(C4)–C5≡N.

questions.title: Rank electronegativity with a less familiar metal
body: Which order is decreasing electronegativity? Use the main-group trend.

blocks: B. F > S > Si > Ba
Why: Electronegativity generally increases up and right; S is to the right of Si.

questions.title: Bond polarity and ionic character
body: Data: EN(H)=2.1, C=2.5, N=3.0, O=3.5. Which is decreasing bond polarity (and approximate ionic character)?
choices: All are equally polar because H is present

blocks: A. O–H > N–H > C–H
Why: Compare ΔEN: 1.4, 0.9, 0.4. This also corrects the reversed printed inequality in slide 42.

questions.title: Separate electronegativity from ionization energy
body: Select every true statement.
choices: A molecule with at least one polar bond must have a nonzero net dipole.
Electronegativity describes attraction for shared bonding electrons.
In N–F, electron density is drawn toward F.
In O–H, H is δ⁺ and O is δ⁻.
Ionization energy is the energy change for adding an electron to a gaseous atom.

blocks: B, C, D. Electronegativity describes attraction for shared bonding electrons. | In N–F, electron density is drawn toward F. | In O–H, H is δ⁺ and O is δ⁻.
Why: Molecular geometry determines cancellation. Ionization energy concerns removal; electron affinity concerns addition.

questions.title: Choose the zero-dipole molecule
body: Which isolated molecule has zero net dipole?

blocks: D. XeF₄
Why: Opposite lone pairs leave a symmetric square-planar array of identical F ligands in XeF₄.

questions.title: All the nonpolar cases
body: Select every nonpolar molecule in its usual isolated geometry.

blocks: A, B, C, D. CO₂ | XeF₂ | BF₃ | SF₆
Why: Identical symmetric bond dipoles cancel in the first four; the two different ends of COS do not cancel.

questions.title: Symmetry of two planar isomers
body: The diagram shows cis- and trans-1,2-dichloroethene. Which pair correctly identifies their net dipoles?
choices: both zero because both contain the same bonds
both nonzero because C–Cl bonds are polar

blocks: C. cis nonzero; trans zero
Why: The symmetric opposite C–Cl dipoles cancel in trans but reinforce in cis.

questions.figureAlt: Two planar CHCl=CHCl drawings: cis has both Cl on the same side; trans has Cl on opposite sides.

questions.title: Shape and polarity of a mixed-ligand center
body: Which description of CH₂Cl₂ is correct?

blocks: D. Tetrahedral and polar
Why: Four domains around carbon give tetrahedral geometry; unlike ligand sets prevent complete dipole cancellation.

questions.title: A shape name alone does not settle polarity
body: Which comparison is correct?
choices: CHCl₃ is trigonal pyramidal because it has three Cl atoms.
Both must be polar because both contain C–Cl bonds.
CCl₄ and CHCl₃ are both tetrahedral, but only CHCl₃ is polar.
Both are square planar and nonpolar.

blocks: C. CCl₄ and CHCl₃ are both tetrahedral, but only CHCl₃ is polar.
Why: Count all four neighboring atoms, then compare vector cancellation rather than counting only one ligand type.

questions.title: Choose the correct shape-polarity pairs
body: Select every correct pair.

blocks: A, B, D. PCl₅: trigonal bipyramidal, nonpolar. | XeF₂: linear, nonpolar. | BrF₅: square pyramidal, polar.
Why: Count central lone pairs: SF₄ is seesaw; NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal.

questions.title: Count bonds in a ring with a nitrile substituent
body: The drawing is benzonitrile: a six-membered carbon ring with three alternating double bonds, five ring hydrogens, and one –C≡N substituent. How many σ and π bonds are present?
questions.familyTitle: Sigma and pi counts in molecular drawings

blocks: Why: σ: six ring links + five C–H + one ring–C + one C–N = 13. π: three ring + two nitrile = 5.

questions.figureAlt: Explicit alternating-bond benzene ring with five H atoms and a C≡N substituent.

questions.title: Two oxygen-containing aromatic drawings
body: The diagram labels phenol A and anisole B. Which total σ/π counts are correct? All C–H and O–H bonds count.
questions.familyTitle: Sigma and pi counts in molecular drawings

blocks: Why: Phenol has 6 ring + 5 ring C–H + C–O + O–H. Anisole replaces O–H by O–C plus three C–H.

questions.figureAlt: A is phenol C₆H₅–O–H; B is anisole C₆H₅–O–CH₃; ring alternating double bonds are explicit.

questions.title: Audit a styrene bond count
body: For styrene C₆H₅–CH=CH₂, drawn with three alternating ring double bonds, select every correct statement.
choices: The exocyclic C=C bond contains one σ and one π.
Both carbons of the –CH=CH₂ group are sp².
There are 16 σ bonds in the whole molecule.
The ring has three σ and three π bonds total.
questions.familyTitle: Sigma and pi counts in molecular drawings

blocks: A, B, C, D. The exocyclic C=C bond contains one σ and one π. | Both carbons of the –CH=CH₂ group are sp². | There are 16 σ bonds in the whole molecule. | There are 4 π bonds.
Why: The six-membered ring has six σ bonds, not three; include all eight C–H bonds and both side-chain C–C connections.

questions.figureAlt: Benzene ring with three alternating double bonds and –CH=CH₂ substituent.

questions.title: Normal boiling point from one pressure
body: Data: R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹; T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15; normal boiling pressure = 760 torr. Treat ΔHvap as constant.
A liquid has vapor pressure 180.0 torr at 298.0 K and ΔHvap = 32.00 kJ/mol. What is its normal boiling point?

questions.title: Predict a new vapor pressure
body: Data: R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹; T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15; normal boiling pressure = 760 torr. Treat ΔHvap as constant.
A liquid has vapor pressure 100.0 torr at 300.0 K and ΔHvap = 30.00 kJ/mol. What is its pressure at 320.0 K?

blocks: A. 212 torr
Why: ln(P₂/100) = (30000/R)(1/300 − 1/320); exponentiate to obtain about 212 torr.

questions.title: Infer ΔHvap before predicting behavior
body: Data: R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹; T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15; normal boiling pressure = 760 torr. Treat ΔHvap as constant.
A liquid has vapor pressure 80.00 torr at 298.15 K and 240.0 torr at 323.15 K. Which estimate of ΔHvap is correct?

blocks: D. 35.2 kJ/mol
Why: ΔHvap = R ln(240/80)/(1/298.15 − 1/323.15) = 35.2 kJ/mol; use Kelvin and J-to-kJ conversion.

questions.title: Compare similar-mass molecular liquids
body: Which has the highest normal boiling point: propane (44.10 g/mol), dimethyl ether (46.07), or ethanol (46.07)?
choices: All equal because their masses are similar

blocks: B. Ethanol
Why: Ethanol can hydrogen-bond to itself; ether has no O–H donor, and propane is nonpolar.

questions.title: Large nonpolar clouds versus small dipoles
body: I₂ is nonpolar and boils at a much higher temperature than polar HCl. Which explanation is best?
choices: I₂ must form hydrogen bonds because its boiling point is high.
I₂ has a much larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so its dispersion attractions can outweigh those in small HCl.
Every nonpolar substance has stronger attractions than every polar one.

blocks: C. I₂ has a much larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so its dispersion attractions can outweigh those in small HCl.
Why: IMF comparisons require size/polarizability as well as named force categories; there is no universal category-only ranking.

questions.title: Shape and polarizability change boiling point
body: Select every correct prediction or explanation.
choices: A molecule with a permanent dipole always boils higher than every nonpolar molecule.
Boiling ethanol normally breaks its C–O covalent bonds.
For otherwise similar molecules, stronger attractions generally raise boiling point.
n-Pentane boils higher than compact neopentane because its shape allows greater intermolecular contact.
Br₂ boils higher than Cl₂ because it is generally more polarizable.

blocks: C, D, E. For otherwise similar molecules, stronger attractions generally raise boiling point. | n-Pentane boils higher than compact neopentane because its shape allows greater intermolecular contact. | Br₂ boils higher than Cl₂ because it is generally more polarizable.
Why: Contact area and polarizability affect attractions; boiling changes intermolecular organization rather than ordinary covalent connectivity.

questions.title: Compare vapor pressures at one temperature
body: At the same temperature, compare hypothetical liquid samples of CH₃OH, CH₃OCH₃, and CH₃CH₂CH₃, each with equilibrium vapor pressure. Which has the lowest vapor pressure?
