choices: All are equal at the same temperature

blocks: A. CH₃OH
Why: Among these similar-mass molecules, methanol’s hydrogen bonding gives the strongest attraction and lowest vapor pressure.

questions.title: Read vapor-pressure curves
body: The graph shows two pure-liquid vapor-pressure curves and a 760-torr line. Select every true statement over the displayed range.
choices: B’s normal boiling point is 340 K.
A has the lower normal boiling point.
At 320 K, A has the higher vapor pressure.
A necessarily has the stronger intermolecular attractions because its vapor pressure is higher.
The normal boiling points occur where each curve meets 760 torr.

blocks: A, B, C, E. B’s normal boiling point is 340 K. | A has the lower normal boiling point. | At 320 K, A has the higher vapor pressure. | The normal boiling points occur where each curve meets 760 torr.
Why: A reaches 760 torr at 320 K; B at 340 K. Higher vapor pressure at the same T generally indicates easier escape.

questions.figureAlt: Curve A crosses 760 torr at 320 K; curve B crosses at 340 K. A lies above B at a common temperature.

questions.title: External pressure versus saturation vapor pressure
body: A pure liquid at 30°C is moved to a lower-pressure environment, while its temperature is held at 30°C and liquid remains. Which statement is correct?
choices: Its equilibrium vapor pressure at 30°C is unchanged, but its boiling temperature at the lower external pressure is lower.
Its equilibrium vapor pressure equals the new external pressure at every temperature.
Its intermolecular forces become stronger when external pressure falls.
Both equilibrium vapor pressure and normal boiling point must decrease.

blocks: A. Its equilibrium vapor pressure at 30°C is unchanged, but its boiling temperature at the lower external pressure is lower.
Why: Saturation vapor pressure is a function of substance and T; boiling requires matching external pressure.

questions.title: Hydrogen bonding in a pure sample
body: Which pair can each hydrogen-bond to identical molecules in a pure sample?

blocks: C. CH₃OH and CH₃NH₂
Why: Each member needs an appropriate N–H, O–H, or F–H donor plus a suitable acceptor in this introductory model.

questions.title: Donors and acceptors are different roles
body: Select every true statement using the introductory course H-bond model.
choices: CH₃OCH₃ can accept a hydrogen bond from water.
CH₃OH both donates and accepts hydrogen bonds.
CH₃OCH₃ hydrogen-bonds to identical ether molecules because it contains O.
CH₃F is treated as a conventional self-hydrogen-bonding liquid merely because it contains both H and F.

blocks: A, B, E. CH₃OCH₃ can accept a hydrogen bond from water. | CH₃OH both donates and accepts hydrogen bonds. | CH₃NH₂ can hydrogen-bond to itself.
Why: Ether has O lone pairs but no appropriate donor H; carbon-bound H in CH₃F is not H–F.

questions.title: List all forces, not only the strongest
body: Which list gives all major intermolecular force types present in pure liquid methanol?
choices: Dispersion only because the whole molecule is neutral

blocks: A. Dispersion, dipole–dipole, and hydrogen bonding
Why: Every molecule has dispersion; polar methanol also has dipole–dipole attractions and O–H hydrogen bonding.

questions.title: Matter wavelength without a long calculation chain
body: An electron (m = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moves at 1.00 × 10⁶ m/s. Which gives its de Broglie wavelength and the effect of doubling its speed?

blocks: D. 0.727 nm; wavelength halves
Why: λ = h/(mv) = 7.27 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum.

questions.title: Uncertainty and relative precision
body: Use Δx·mΔv ≥ h/(4π). An electron has speed 2.00 × 10⁶ m/s with uncertainty Δv = 0.800% of that speed; m = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What is the minimum Δx, and how does it change if Δv is reduced by a factor of 4?

blocks: C. 3.62 nm; minimum Δx increases by 4
Why: Δv = 1.60 × 10⁴ m/s. The uncertainty-product bound makes the minimum Δx inversely proportional to Δv.

questions.title: Orbitals, nodes, shielding, and penetration
body: Select every correct statement in the course atomic model.
choices: Inner electrons effectively shield outer electrons from the full nuclear charge.
For a typical multielectron atom at fixed n, s generally lies below p because of greater penetration.
The two lobes of one p orbital are two separate orbitals.
For isolated H, 3s, 3p, and 3d are degenerate in the model.

blocks: A, B, C, E. A 4s orbital has 3 total nodes. | Inner electrons effectively shield outer electrons from the full nuclear charge. | For a typical multielectron atom at fixed n, s generally lies below p because of greater penetration. | For isolated H, 3s, 3p, and 3d are degenerate in the model.
Why: Total nodes = n−1. Shielding/penetration split same-n subshell energies in multielectron atoms.

questions.title: Inert-pair and pseudo-noble-gas configurations
body: Sn has [Kr]4d¹⁰5s²5p². Which comparison is correct?
choices: Both ions are isoelectronic with Xe.
Sn²⁺ is [Kr]4d¹⁰5s² (inert pair); Sn⁴⁺ is [Kr]4d¹⁰ (pseudo-noble gas).
Sn²⁺ has two unpaired 5p electrons and must be paramagnetic.

blocks: B. Sn²⁺ is [Kr]4d¹⁰5s² (inert pair); Sn⁴⁺ is [Kr]4d¹⁰ (pseudo-noble gas).
Why: Remove highest-n p electrons first, then s. The retained 5s² pair and filled d¹⁰ configuration have distinct lecture names.

questions.title: Electron-affinity signs and a familiar exception
body: Use signed electron affinities for X(g)+e⁻→X⁻(g): EA(F)=−328, EA(Cl)=−349 kJ/mol. Select every correct statement.
choices: Adding an electron to Cl releases more energy than adding one to F.
The data prove that EA becomes steadily more negative going upward in every group.
Adding a second electron to O⁻(g) ordinarily requires energy.
The more negative EA is the more exothermic addition.
IE and EA are the same process with the same sign.

blocks: A, C, D. Adding an electron to Cl releases more energy than adding one to F. | Adding a second electron to O⁻(g) ordinarily requires energy. | The more negative EA is the more exothermic addition.
Why: EA trends have exceptions; gas-phase addition to an already negative ion opposes electrostatic repulsion.

questions.title: Covalent radius versus nonbonded contact
body: The Cl–Cl covalent bond length is 198 pm; closest nonbonded Cl···Cl contact is 360 pm. An additive covalent-radius model gives C–Cl = 176 pm. Which set is correct?
choices: r covalent(Cl)=99 pm; r vdW(Cl)=180 pm; r covalent(C)=77 pm

blocks: C. r covalent(Cl)=99 pm; r vdW(Cl)=180 pm; r covalent(C)=77 pm
Why: Each identical-atom distance is twice the corresponding radius. Use covalent, not van der Waals, radius in the C–Cl bond estimate.

questions.title: Light and quantum-model evidence
body: Select every true statement.
choices: An orbital specifies a definite circular electron path.
Planck’s oscillator model permits energy changes in integer multiples of hν.
Higher amplitude can raise light intensity without changing its frequency.
Radio has higher photon energy than ultraviolet.

blocks: B, C, F. Planck’s oscillator model permits energy changes in integer multiples of hν. | Higher amplitude can raise light intensity without changing its frequency. | Diffraction demonstrates wave behavior.
Why: Wave interference/diffraction and quantized energy exchange are complementary evidence; E varies inversely with wavelength.

questions.title: Bonding models and conductivity
body: Select every correct statement about pure Cu, NaCl, and CH₃OH.
choices: Cu has metallic bonding and mobile electrons that carry current.
Molten NaCl can conduct because ions are mobile.
CH₃OH has covalent bonds within molecules and intermolecular attractions between them.
Solid NaCl conducts well because its ions are charged even when fixed.
An ionic crystal can fracture when displacement places like charges next to one another.

blocks: A, B, C, E. Cu has metallic bonding and mobile electrons that carry current. | Molten NaCl can conduct because ions are mobile. | CH₃OH has covalent bonds within molecules and intermolecular attractions between them. | An ionic crystal can fracture when displacement places like charges next to one another.
Why: Charge carriers must be mobile. Ionic solids are extended lattices, whereas methanol consists of covalent molecules.

questions.title: Lattice attraction: charge and separation
body: Use U ∝ |z₊z₋|/r and define U as positive lattice-separation energy. MgO: charges ±2, r=212 pm; NaCl: charges ±1, r=282 pm. Which result is correct, assuming equal structural factors?
choices: Ratio ≈ 0.188; lattice formation has negative ΔE.
Ratio ≈ 1.33; lattice formation has positive ΔE.
U(MgO)/U(NaCl) ≈ 5.32; lattice formation has negative ΔE.

blocks: D. U(MgO)/U(NaCl) ≈ 5.32; lattice formation has negative ΔE.
Why: (4/212)/(1/282)=5.32. Forming the lattice is the reverse of energy-requiring separation.

questions.title: Bond order, length, and strength
body: For the same C–C atom pair in comparable environments, which ordering and explanation are correct?
choices: Length: C≡C < C=C < C–C; higher bond order generally means a stronger bond.
All three lengths are equal because the atom types are the same.
Length: C–C < C=C < C≡C; all σ bonds are longer than all π bonds.
A double bond is exactly twice as strong as a single bond.

blocks: A. Length: C≡C < C=C < C–C; higher bond order generally means a stronger bond.
Why: Additional bonding generally increases attraction and shortens a comparable bond; π and σ components are not identical in strength.

questions.title: Formal charge is not oxidation number
body: For the octet structure :C≡O: (one lone pair on each atom), which statement is correct? Assign C–O electrons to O for oxidation numbers.
choices: The molecule contains a free C²⁺ ion and a free O²⁻ ion.
Both atoms have zero formal charge and oxidation number.
FC(C)=−1, FC(O)=+1; oxidation numbers C=+2, O=−2.
FC(C)=+2, FC(O)=−2; oxidation numbers C=−1, O=+1.

blocks: C. FC(C)=−1, FC(O)=+1; oxidation numbers C=+2, O=−2.
Why: Formal charge splits bonds equally; oxidation-number bookkeeping assigns their electrons to the more electronegative atom.

questions.title: Choose unequal resonance contributors
body: NCO⁻ has two octet contributors: A N≡C–O with formal charges (0,0,−1), B N=C=O with (−1,0,0). O is more electronegative than N. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: B contributes more because N must always carry a negative charge.
A contributes more; an unweighted bond-order average is not exact.
A and B are different molecules because their electron positions differ.
Both must contribute equally because their total charges match.

blocks: B. A contributes more; an unweighted bond-order average is not exact.
Why: Negative charge is preferred on O when octets and charge magnitudes otherwise compare equally.

questions.title: Identify all three octet exceptions
body: Select every correct statement. Valence electrons: B3, N5, O6, F7, P5, Cl7.
choices: BF₃ is electron-deficient at B in its usual introductory Lewis structure.
An ordinary NCl₅ structure with five single bonds is an allowed second-period expanded octet.
Every neutral molecule must have an even number of valence electrons.
PCl₅ is represented with an expanded valence shell at P.
NO₂ has 17 valence electrons and must have an unpaired electron.

blocks: A, D, E. BF₃ is electron-deficient at B in its usual introductory Lewis structure. | PCl₅ is represented with an expanded valence shell at P. | NO₂ has 17 valence electrons and must have an unpaired electron.
Why: Incomplete octets, odd-electron radicals, and expanded valence shells are different exceptions; second-period N does not expand its octet.

questions.title: Oxyacid formal-charge preference
body: H₃PO₄ has P bonded to four O atoms, three bearing H. Compare all P–O single bonds with O=P(OH)₃. Which result follows the lecture Lewis conventions?
choices: The P=O double bond creates a fifth VSEPR domain.
All-single-bond P has FC=−1 and the unprotonated O has FC=+1.
H₃PO₄ must be square planar because it has four O atoms.
The P=O drawing has all formal charges zero; both drawings have four P-centered domains.

blocks: D. The P=O drawing has all formal charges zero; both drawings have four P-centered domains.
Why: The all-single-bond form has P +1 and unprotonated O −1; using P=O removes those charges without changing the four neighbor directions.

questions.title: Promotion, mixing, and the remaining p orbital
body: The diagram shows a four-electron carbon sp² construction. Select every true statement.
choices: The π component of an ethene double bond comes from sideways p–p overlap.
Three atomic orbitals mix to give three sp² orbitals.
One p orbital remains outside the hybrid set.
Hybridization mixes orbitals from two different carbon atoms into one atom’s hybrid set.
The four valence electrons are conserved through the construction.

blocks: A, B, C, E. The π component of an ethene double bond comes from sideways p–p overlap. | Three atomic orbitals mix to give three sp² orbitals. | One p orbital remains outside the hybrid set. | The four valence electrons are conserved through the construction.
Why: Hybridization combines orbitals on one atom; overlap between atoms subsequently describes bonding. Promotion is schematic valence-bond bookkeeping.

questions.figureAlt: Carbon ground 2s²2p², promoted 2s¹2p³, then three singly occupied sp² orbitals plus one singly occupied p orbital.

questions.title: Bond-energy changes versus bond breaking
body: Data: H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)→2HCl(g). Average bond energies: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol. Use ΔH≈ΣD(broken)−ΣD(formed). Which estimate and interpretation are correct?
choices: +183 kJ; exothermic because breaking bonds releases energy.
−183 kJ per mole of reaction; exothermic because forming two H–Cl bonds releases more energy than breaking the reactant bonds costs.
+679 kJ; product formation has no energy change.

blocks: C. −183 kJ per mole of reaction; exothermic because forming two H–Cl bonds releases more energy than breaking the reactant bonds costs.
Why: 436+243−2(431)=−183 kJ/mol. Breaking costs energy and forming releases energy.

questions.title: Dispersion and molecular contact
body: Select every true statement.
choices: For similar nonpolar particles, larger polarizability generally strengthens dispersion.
Nonpolar molecules still have London dispersion attractions.
Permanent dipoles are required for any intermolecular attraction.
Equal molar masses guarantee equal boiling points.
Elongated n-pentane can contact neighbors more effectively than compact neopentane.

blocks: A, B, E. For similar nonpolar particles, larger polarizability generally strengthens dispersion. | Nonpolar molecules still have London dispersion attractions. | Elongated n-pentane can contact neighbors more effectively than compact neopentane.
Why: Instantaneous and induced dipoles exist even without a permanent molecular dipole; molecular shape also matters.

questions.title: Latent heat needs moles
body: At 0°C, ΔHfus(H₂O)=6.01 kJ/mol. How much heat is absorbed by melting 27.02 g ice at 0°C, and does the temperature rise while both phases coexist at fixed pressure? M(H₂O)=18.015 g/mol.

blocks: B. 9.01 kJ; no
Why: q=(27.02/18.015)×6.01=9.01 kJ. During a constant-pressure transition the energy changes phase amounts rather than T.

questions.title: Headspace and dynamic equilibrium
body: A closed flask has pure liquid and its equilibrium vapor at fixed T. Enough liquid remains after headspace volume doubles. Select every correct statement after equilibrium returns.
choices: If all liquid were exhausted, remaining gas would still necessarily have the saturation pressure.
The amount of vapor doubles in the ideal-gas approximation.
Evaporation and condensation occur at equal rates.

blocks: B, C, D. The amount of vapor doubles in the ideal-gas approximation. | Evaporation and condensation occur at equal rates. | Saturation vapor pressure is unchanged.
Why: At fixed T and saturation P, n=PV/RT scales with headspace volume, provided liquid remains.

questions.title: Phase-diagram exceptions
body: Use the CO₂ phase diagram: triple point −56.6°C, 5.11 atm; critical point 31.0°C, 73.0 atm. Select every correct statement.
choices: The critical point is where solid, liquid, and gas all coexist.
At 40°C and 90 atm, CO₂ is supercritical.
All three phases coexist at the triple point.
At 1 atm, solid CO₂ sublimes rather than forming an equilibrium liquid.
Pressure alone at 40°C can create an ordinary liquid–gas coexistence transition.

blocks: B, C, D. At 40°C and 90 atm, CO₂ is supercritical. | All three phases coexist at the triple point. | At 1 atm, solid CO₂ sublimes rather than forming an equilibrium liquid.
Why: Liquid is not stable below the triple pressure, and the liquid–gas boundary ends at the critical point.

questions.figureAlt: Schematic CO₂ pressure-temperature diagram with the triple and critical points labeled.

questions.title: Water’s negative melting-line slope
body: Near 0°C, ice is less dense than liquid water and the solid–liquid coexistence line slopes negatively in a P–T diagram. Which response follows a small pressure increase near this boundary?
choices: Ice is favored and the melting point increases.
Pressure cannot affect a melting equilibrium.
Liquid is favored and the melting point decreases.
Liquid is favored and the melting point increases.

blocks: C. Liquid is favored and the melting point decreases.
Why: Increasing pressure favors the smaller-volume phase, here liquid water.

questions.title: States and phase-change signs
body: Select every true statement about ordinary molecular phases.
choices: A liquid has nearly fixed volume but takes the shape of its occupied container region.
Sublimation absorbs heat; deposition releases heat.
Particles in a solid have zero kinetic energy.
A pure substance can have liquid and vapor phases simultaneously.

blocks: A, B, E. A liquid has nearly fixed volume but takes the shape of its occupied container region. | Sublimation absorbs heat; deposition releases heat. | A pure substance can have liquid and vapor phases simultaneously.
Why: Particles still move in solids. Vaporization, fusion, and sublimation are endothermic.

questions.title: Read a Clausius-Clapeyron slope
body: A plot of ln(P) versus 1/T (T in K) has slope −4200 K. What is ΔHvap? R=8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹.

blocks: A. 34.9 kJ/mol
Why: Slope = −ΔHvap/R; multiply 4200 by 8.314 J/mol·K and divide by 1000.

questions.title: Orient water around ions
body: Which orientation and force description is correct for water near Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻?
choices: H ends toward Ca²⁺; O end toward Cl⁻; ion–dipole in both cases.
O end toward Ca²⁺; H ends toward Cl⁻; ion–dipole in both cases.
H ends toward both ions; covalent bonding in both cases.
O end toward both ions; dispersion only.

blocks: B. O end toward Ca²⁺; H ends toward Cl⁻; ion–dipole in both cases.
Why: Opposite charge regions attract: water’s oxygen is δ⁻ and its hydrogen ends δ⁺.

questions.title: Potassium photoelectric threshold
body: Data from the review sheet: h=6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; c=3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.
The binding energy for potassium is 3.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Which is the longest wavelength which could eject an electron from the potassium surface?

blocks: B. 540 nm
Why: hc/Ebinding ≈ 540 nm; longer wavelengths carry insufficient photon energy.

questions.title: Shortest-wavelength hydrogen emission
body: Which electronic transition in a hydrogen atom corresponds to emission of the shortest-wavelength photon?

blocks: Why: The 3 → 1 transition has the largest downward energy gap of those listed.

questions.title: Allowed quantum-number combinations
body: Which combination of quantum numbers is not allowed?

blocks: B. n=1, ℓ=1, mℓ=0, mₛ=−½
Why: For n=1, only ℓ=0 is allowed.

questions.title: An occupied magnetic quantum number
body: How many electrons in a ground-state argon atom can have mℓ=+1?

blocks: Why: The filled 2p and 3p subshells each contribute two; s orbitals have mℓ=0.

questions.title: Increasing-radius series
body: Which series is correctly arranged in increasing radius?

blocks: A. Ca²⁺ < K⁺ < Ar < Cl⁻ < S²⁻
Why: All five species have 18 electrons; increasing nuclear charge gives decreasing size in this isoelectronic comparison.

questions.title: Silicon’s ionization-energy jump
body: A large jump in silicon’s successive ionization energies occurs between which two values?

blocks: D. IE₄ and IE₅
Why: Si has four valence electrons; the fifth removal reaches a core electron.

questions.title: Choose a paramagnetic ion
body: Which ion is paramagnetic? Use isolated ground-state ions and Hund’s-rule d occupancy.

blocks: D. Co²⁺
Why: Co²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁷ with unpaired electrons; the other ions listed are closed shell.

questions.title: Which pair has different configurations?
body: Which pair does not have identical ground-state electron configurations?

blocks: B. Ni and Cu⁺
Why: Ni is [Ar]3d⁸4s²; Cu⁺ is [Ar]3d¹⁰. Their electron counts match but their configurations differ.

questions.title: Best COCl₂ Lewis structure
body: Select the best Lewis structure for COCl₂ from the four panels.

blocks: D. Panel D
Why: D has 24 valence electrons, octets on C/O/Cl, and zero formal charges. In the supplied diagram B is missing an O lone pair.

questions.figureAlt: Four COCl₂ Lewis-structure options A-D, reproduced from the supplied question; lone-pair dots are essential.

questions.title: Formula and charge from a Lewis drawing
body: What is the formula for the following Lewis structure?
questions.familyTitle: Infer a formula or charge from a drawing

blocks: B. CNO⁻
Why: The displayed O≡C–N structure has 16 electrons, one more than the neutral valence sum of 15.

questions.figureAlt: O≡C–N with one O lone pair and three N lone pairs.

questions.title: Formal charge on nitrogen
body: The formal charge on N in a major octet Lewis structure of NO₂⁻ is:

blocks: Why: N has one lone pair and total bond order 3: 5−2−3=0.

questions.title: Carbonate resonance forms
body: Carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻, has how many equivalent major resonance forms?

blocks: Why: The C=O bond can be placed at any of three equivalent O sites.

questions.title: Shape of a mixed-ligand chlorine center
body: What is the molecular shape of ClO₃F as predicted by VSEPR theory for the displayed structure?

blocks: D. Tetrahedral
Why: Four bonded neighbors and no central lone pair give AX₄; multiple bonds count as one domain each.

questions.figureAlt: Supplied ClO₃F Lewis drawing with Cl bonded to three O atoms and one F atom.

questions.title: Angle in PH₂⁻
body: What is the H–P–H bond angle in PH₂⁻, according to the lecture VSEPR model?

blocks: A. Less than 109.5°
Why: Two bonds and two lone pairs give tetrahedral electron geometry and a bent shape with compressed bond angle.

questions.title: Hybridization in SnCl₃⁻
body: Valence bond theory predicts that tin uses which hybrid orbitals in SnCl₃⁻?

blocks: C. sp³
Why: Three bonds plus one central lone pair give four domains and the sp³ lecture-model label.

questions.title: Right-most carbon hybridization
body: Which hybridization describes the right-most carbon atom in the molecule below?

blocks: A. sp
Why: The nitrile carbon has two σ-domain directions; the triple bond’s π components do not add domains.

questions.figureAlt: The supplied structure is CH₃–C(=O)–CH₂–C≡N; the right-most carbon is the nitrile carbon.

questions.title: Decreasing electronegativity
body: Arrange fluorine, silicon, sulfur, and barium in decreasing electronegativity.

blocks: C. F > S > Si > Ba
Why: F is highest; S lies to the right of Si, and Ba is a low-electronegativity metal.

questions.title: Zero molecular dipole
body: Which molecule has a zero dipole moment?

blocks: C. BF₃
Why: BF₃ is symmetric trigonal planar; its three B–F bond dipoles cancel.

questions.title: CH₂Cl₂: shape and polarity
body: CH₂Cl₂ is a ______ molecule and its molecular shape is ______.

blocks: B. Polar; tetrahedral
Why: Four electron domains give tetrahedral geometry; the mixed H/Cl ligands prevent cancellation.

questions.title: Sigma and pi bonds in phenol
body: There are how many σ and π bonds, respectively, in the phenol molecule?
questions.familyTitle: Sigma and pi counts in molecular drawings

blocks: Why: Six ring σ + five C–H + C–O + O–H = 13 σ; the three ring double bonds add 3 π.

questions.figureAlt: The supplied phenol drawing shows six ring carbons, five ring hydrogens, and an O–H substituent.

questions.title: Normal boiling point from vapor-pressure data
body: A liquid has ΔHvap=17.2 kJ/mol. At 285 K its vapor pressure is 212 torr. What is its normal boiling point? R=8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹.

blocks: Why: The two-point Clausius–Clapeyron relation gives about 346 K, or 73°C.

questions.title: Highest boiling point among the listed substances

Use solid boundaries for included points and dashed boundaries for excluded points. Keep the original restrictions when squaring or solving for a level.
The range is the set of attained output values. Check endpoints rather than assuming they are included.
Level curves satisfy \(f(x,y)=k\); level surfaces satisfy \(f(x,y,z)=k\). They live in input space. Vertical traces use \(x=a\) or \(y=b\).
For equal height steps, closer contours indicate steeper change. Check the labels and scale.

guides.title: Brief continuity review
body: Continuity at \((a,b)\) requires \(\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)}f(x,y)=f(a,b)\), through every path in the domain.
Two paths with different limits prove that the limit does not exist. Agreement along a few paths does not prove that a limit exists.
For continuous elementary functions, substitute directly where the expression is defined.
Partial derivatives can exist even when the function is not continuous; see question 14.3.8.

guides.title: Partial derivatives
body: Hold the other variables constant and apply the usual product, quotient, and chain rules.
\(f_x\) and \(f_y\) are coordinate trace slopes, not function heights.
\(f_{xy}=(f_x)_y\). Continuous mixed second partials can be interchanged. Differentiate repeatedly before substituting a point.
If \(F(x,y,z)=0\) defines \(z\) locally and \(F_z\ne0\), then \(z_x=-F_x/F_z\) and \(z_y=-F_y/F_z\).
When computing \(F_x,F_y,F_z\), hold the other inputs constant. When differentiating the identity, remember that \(z\) depends on \(x,y\).
Existence of partial derivatives alone does not guarantee continuity or differentiability.

guides.title: Tangent planes and linear approximations
body: Linearization: \(L(x,y)=f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)(x-a)+f_y(a,b)(y-b)\). The tangent plane is \(z=L(x,y)\).
Differential: \(df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy\), with an additional \(f_z\,dz\) term for three inputs.
\(\Delta f\) is the exact new value minus the old value; \(df\) approximates it.
Estimated maximum error: \(|df|\le|f_x|\varepsilon_x+|f_y|\varepsilon_y\). Relative error is \(|df|/|f|\); multiply by \(100\) for a percentage.
Continuous first partials near the point guarantee differentiability. A zero partial means no first-order contribution, not necessarily zero actual change.

guides.title: Chain rule and related rates
body: Along a path, \(df/dt=f_xx'+f_yy'+f_zz'\).
For two parameters, \(f_s=f_xx_s+f_yy_s+f_zz_s\), and similarly for \(f_t\). Include every dependency path.
In \(G(u(s,t),v(s,t))\), evaluate the outer derivatives \(G_u,G_v\) at \((u,v)\), not at \((s,t)\).
For \(F(x,y)=0\), implicit differentiation gives \(y'=-F_x/F_y\) when \(F_y\ne0\).
Use signed rates and consistent units in related-rate problems. With explicit time dependence, \(dT/dt=T_xx'+T_yy'+T_t\).
Change per unit time and change per unit distance are different quantities.

guides.title: Directional derivatives and gradients
body: The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives. For a unit vector \(\mathbf u\), \(D_{\mathbf u}f=\nabla f\cdot\mathbf u\).
Toward \(Q\) from \(P\), normalize \(Q-P\) before taking the dot product.

Maximum rate: \(\|
abla f\|\), in direction \(
abla f/\|
abla f\|\). Minimum rate: \(-\|
abla f\|\), in the opposite direction. Perpendicular directions have zero rate.
For \(F=c\) with nonzero gradient, the tangent plane is \(\nabla F(P)\cdot(\mathbf r-P)=0\); the normal line is \(\mathbf r=P+t\nabla F(P)\).
Along a path, \(df/dt=\nabla f\cdot\mathbf r'\). A zero directional derivative at one point does not make a straight path a level curve.

guides.title: Local and absolute extrema
body: Critical points satisfy \(f_x=f_y=0\), or occur where a partial is undefined. A candidate need not be an extremum.
With continuous second partials, let \(D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-(f_{xy})^2\).
If \(D>0\) and \(f_{xx}>0\): local minimum. If \(D>0\) and \(f_{xx}<0\): local maximum. If \(D<0\): saddle. If \(D=0\): inconclusive.
A continuous function on a closed bounded region attains absolute extrema. Check interior candidates, every boundary segment, and endpoints; compare original function values.
When \(D=0\), use signs, factorization, sums of squares, or paths. State the extremal values and all attaining points.
A nonstrict minimum permits nearby points with equal values; a strict minimum does not.

guides.title: Lagrange multipliers
body:
For one constraint \(g=c\), solve \(
abla f=\lambda
abla g\) with the constraint. The usual condition is \(
abla g
e\mathbf0\); check exceptional points separately.
Do not divide by variables or multipliers before checking their zero cases. A finite candidate list does not guarantee absolute extrema on an unbounded set.
For a region \(g\le c\), check both the interior and the boundary.
Optimize squared distance first, then take its square root. Include all physical restrictions in applied problems.

With two constraints, solve \(
abla f=\lambda
abla g+\mu
abla h\) together with both constraints. The constraint gradients must be linearly independent.

guides.title: Top-down design and dictionaries
body: Start with the whole goal, divide it into coherent major tasks, and refine each task until its implementation is clear. Sibling tasks should have distinct responsibilities. Several reasonable decompositions may exist.

Root: no parent. Node: any element. Parent/child: adjacent levels. Leaf: no children. A leaf does not have to be on the deepest level. Hierarchies manage complexity but can hide connections across branches.

A dictionary maps keys to values. Keys are unique; values may repeat. d[key] looks up a key, not a position. Assigning an existing key replaces its value; assigning a new key adds a pair. Accessing a missing key raises KeyError.

key in d checks exact keys, not values or substrings. for key in d iterates over keys; use d[key] to read each corresponding value. len(d) counts pairs. Update existing values freely; avoid adding/deleting keys while directly iterating over the dictionary.
Initialize a missing key once; update on every occurrence. Do not reset a count each time you see the key.

Lecture 8 teaches {}, key indexing/assignment, membership, and direct iteration. This bank does not require get, items, values, pop, dictionary comprehensions, or other methods from a broader dictionary guide.
Source: Lecture8.pdf pp11-18,19-25,28-32

guides.title: Functions, scope, and shared objects
body: def records a function; its body runs when called. Parameters are the local names in the header; arguments are supplied at the call. return immediately exits the function. print displays text; it does not substitute for returning a result. Reaching the end without return gives None.
return a, b returns one tuple. x, y = f() unpacks by position. Tuple indexing and slicing work, but replacing a tuple slot raises TypeError. A mutable list stored inside a tuple can still change.

Each call gets local parameter/variable bindings. Reassigning a numeric or string parameter does not change the caller variable. A function can read a global if not shadowed; assigning to a name makes it local unless declared global. Reading such a local before assigning it raises UnboundLocalError.

a[0] = 9 changes a shared list; a = [9] only rebinds local a. For lists, a += [9] mutates while a = a + [9] rebinds. Dictionaries also share mutations through passed references. b = a aliases a list; b = a[:] makes a new outer list, not a recursive copy of nested lists.

Omitted trailing arguments use defaults; an explicit zero does not. In the taught positional headers, required parameters precede defaulted ones. Put a docstring first in the body describing purpose, inputs, outputs, and relevant units. Prefer arguments and returned results over hidden global dependencies.

Bind arguments -> run the body in order -> track shared-object mutations separately -> stop at return -> assign/use the returned object in the caller. Keep a separate row of local variables for every call.

body.code:
def split_total(total, people=2):
    """Return equal integer share and leftover units."""
    return total // people, total % people
share, leftover = split_total(17, 5)  # 3, 2
