guides.title: Atomic structure & periodic trends
body: Use the new MCQ families and retained lecture-coverage questions for this chapter; the Concept / pattern filter groups three variants of each professor-review type.

sections.title: Light, spectra, and photons
body: \(c=\lambda\nu\), \(E_{\rm photon}=h\nu=hc/\lambda\). Convert wavelength to meters before using SI constants. Shorter wavelength → higher frequency → higher photon energy. Spectrum from low to high energy: radio, microwave, infrared, visible (red → violet), ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

Amplitude affects intensity, not frequency. Diffraction/interference reveal wave behavior; quantized energy exchange and the photoelectric effect reveal photon behavior. A hot object’s broad spectrum differs from an isolated atom’s discrete absorption/emission lines.
Photon count: \(N=E_{\rm total}/E_{\rm photon}\). A light source of power P delivers energy \(Pt\). Energy per mole of photons is \(N_AE_{\rm photon}\).

Planck’s quantization model restricts an oscillator’s energy to integer multiples of hν: E = nhν. Energy is exchanged in discrete quanta rather than arbitrary amounts; this resolves the classical failure to describe blackbody radiation. Distinguish this oscillator n from the hydrogen principal quantum number in the Bohr formula.

sections.title: Photoelectric effect
body:
\(K_{\max}=h
u-\phi\); threshold \(
u_0=\phi/h\), \(\lambda_0=hc/\phi\). Ejection requires \(
u\ge
u_0\) or \(\lambda\le\lambda_0\); at threshold the ideal maximum kinetic energy is zero.

Above threshold, greater intensity at fixed frequency increases the emission rate, not the maximum electron kinetic energy. Below threshold, greater intensity does not fix the problem in the ordinary single-photon model. Use K = ½mv² to connect electron energy and speed.

sections.title: Bohr energy levels and transitions
body: For H: \(E_n=-R_H/n^2\), with \(R_H=2.179\times10^{-18}\ {\rm J}\). \(\Delta E_{\rm atom}=E_f-E_i\). Absorption: positive ΔE and larger n. Emission: negative ΔE and smaller n. Photon energy is always the positive magnitude \(|\Delta E|\).

n = 1 is the ground state; higher bound n values are excited states. Ionization takes the electron to E = 0 (n → ∞). The energy needed from level n is R_H/n². Only discrete matching photon energies cause bound-to-bound transitions.

For hydrogen, transitions ending at n = 1 are ultraviolet; the common n ≥ 3 → 2 lines are visible; transitions ending at n = 3 are infrared. Cascade energies add; wavelengths do not. The Bohr model is useful for H energy calculations, but literal circular paths are not quantum-mechanical orbitals.

sections.title: Matter waves and uncertainty
body: \(\lambda=h/(mv)\); mass must be kg. Greater momentum means shorter de Broglie wavelength. If kinetic energy is given, use \(mv=\sqrt{2mK}\). Wave effects are most observable for tiny particles.

\(\Delta x\,m\Delta v\ge h/(4\pi)\). A percent uncertainty multiplies the stated speed: 0.8% means 0.008v. Better-defined momentum means less-defined position. This is a quantum limit, not just poor equipment.

sections.title: Orbitals, shapes, and quantum numbers
body: An orbital is a wavefunction, not a track. |ψ|² gives probability density. Nodes have zero probability density; the lecture’s total-node rule is n − 1. s orbitals are spherical; p orbitals have two lobes; most d orbitals have four lobes, while d_z² has two lobes and a torus.

n = 1, 2, 3, …; ℓ = 0 through n − 1; mℓ = −ℓ through +ℓ; mₛ = ±½. ℓ = 0, 1, 2, 3 corresponds to s, p, d, f. An orbital is specified by the first three numbers; a particular electron requires all four.

A subshell has \(2\ell+1\) orbitals and capacity \(2(2\ell+1)\) electrons. A shell has \(n^2\) orbitals and capacity \(2n^2\). For partially specified quantum numbers, count every allowed combination of the missing numbers.

sections.title: Orbital energy and filling
body: Hydrogen orbitals with the same n have equal energy in the course model. In multielectron atoms, shielding and penetration split subshell energies. For a fixed n, s penetrates most and usually has the lowest energy: s < p < d < f. Increasing nuclear attraction generally lowers electron energy.

Aufbau: fill lower-energy available orbitals first. Pauli: at most two electrons per orbital with opposite spins. Hund: fill equal-energy orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing. Common order: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p.
Period-4 exceptions: Cr [Ar] 3d⁵4s¹ and Cu [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s¹. Distinguish a forbidden Pauli arrangement from an allowed excited configuration that is not the ground state.

sections.title: Configurations, ions, and magnetism
body: For ions, count electrons from atomic number and charge. Remove the highest-n electrons first: transition metals lose ns before (n − 1)d, even though ns was filled first. Main-group ions often, but not always, reach a noble-gas configuration.

Main-group valence electrons occupy the highest n shell. In the lecture’s transition-metal convention, valence includes ns and (n − 1)d electrons. The d-block subshell has n = period − 1; the f-block subshell has n = period − 2.
Pseudo-noble-gas ions retain filled d¹⁰ beneath an empty outer shell; inert-pair ions retain ns². Example: Sn⁴⁺ = [Kr] 4d¹⁰, Sn²⁺ = [Kr] 4d¹⁰5s². Neither is a noble-gas configuration.

At least one unpaired electron → paramagnetic; all paired → diamagnetic. Draw the orbital occupancy rather than relying on total electron parity. For the isolated ions in this review, use Hund’s rule; coordination-complex spin splitting is outside this review.

sections.title: Size, ionization energy, and electron affinity
body: Atomic radius generally increases down a group and decreases across a main-group period. Effective nuclear attraction grows across a period. Cations are smaller than their parent atoms; anions are larger. Among isoelectronic ions, more protons means smaller radius. Do not apply this rule to ions with different shell populations without checking n.

IE is positive for removing an electron from a gaseous species. IE₁ generally increases across and decreases down. The large jump in successive IE occurs after all valence electrons have been removed. Add successive IE values when removing several electrons. Be/B and N/O illustrate subshell and pairing exceptions.

Here EA means the signed energy change for X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g): favorable electron addition usually has negative EA. More negative means more energy released; avoid ambiguous phrases such as “larger affinity.” EA trends are less regular than radius/IE trends. Adding a second electron to an already negative gas-phase ion requires energy.

Covalent radius is half the distance in an identical-atom covalent bond; metallic radius is half the nearest metal-atom separation. Van der Waals radius comes from nonbonded contact and is larger than the corresponding covalent radius.

sections.title: Source coverage & accuracy notes
body: Scope: Chapter 6 slides 3–40 (light/H), 41–50 (matter waves/uncertainty), 51–89 (quantum model/configurations), 90–100 (ions/magnetism), 101–124 (periodic properties). Style calibrated against the supplied Quizzes 2–3 and Chapter 6–8 homework; no past test paper was supplied for this update. Questions here are original practice.

Accuracy note: Chapter 6 slide 50 mixes two electron speeds in its worked uncertainty example. Use the stated speed. The pasted radio-photon result is consistent: 2.44 × 10⁻²⁴ J corresponds to about 8.15 cm with the quiz constants.

guides.title: Bonding, Lewis structures & molecular shape
body: Use the new MCQ families and retained lecture-coverage questions for this chapter; the Concept / pattern filter groups three variants of each professor-review type.

sections.title: Three bonding models
body: Ionic: oppositely charged ions held in a lattice. Covalent: shared electron density between nuclei. Metallic: metal centers held together by delocalized electrons. Many substances have bonding within particles and separate forces between particles.

Ionic solids are rigid and brittle and usually have high melting points. Fixed ions cannot carry current through the solid; mobile ions carry current in melts and soluble ionic solutions. Metals conduct through mobile electrons. Molecular substances usually lack mobile charge carriers.

sections.title: Lattice energy and covalent bond properties
body: The slides define lattice energy as positive energy to separate a solid into gaseous ions. The reverse releases energy. Approximate comparison: \(|U|\propto |z_+z_-|/r\); larger ionic charges and shorter separations strengthen attraction.

For the same atom pair: higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond. Single/double/triple bonds contain 1/2/3 shared pairs. A double bond is not exactly twice as strong as a single bond; bond-energy values depend on the surrounding molecule.

When average bond energies are supplied, \(\Delta H_{\rm rxn}\approx\sum D(\text{broken})-\sum D(\text{formed})\). Breaking costs energy; forming releases it. Count stoichiometric bonds, cancel unchanged ones if helpful, and scale by moles actually reacting. Average gas-phase bond energies give estimates.

sections.title: Electronegativity and bond polarity
body: Electronegativity measures attraction for shared electrons. It generally increases across a period and decreases down a group; F is highest. The more electronegative end is δ⁻; the chemistry bond-dipole arrow points toward it.
Larger ΔEN generally means greater bond polarity and ionic character. There is no universal sharp boundary. Bond polarity is not the same as molecular polarity: geometry determines cancellation.
Correction to slide 42: decreasing ionic character for those examples is H–O > H–N > H–C. The printed inequality in the slide is reversed.

sections.title: Lewis structure workflow
body: 1. Count valence electrons; add for negative charge and subtract for positive charge. 2. Choose the connectivity (H is terminal; the less electronegative non-H atom is often central). 3. Add single bonds. 4. Complete terminal octets, then put leftovers on the center. 5. Form multiple bonds if needed for an allowed central octet.

Show lone pairs, brackets, and the overall charge of ions. H has a duet. Keep the given connectivity; resonance moves electrons, not atoms. For several centers, analyze each local environment separately.

sections.title: Formal charge, resonance, and oxidation number
body: \(\mathrm{FC}=V-N-\tfrac12 B\), where V is neutral-atom valence electrons, N is nonbonding electrons, and B is bonding electrons. Equivalently subtract the sum of bond orders from V − N. Formal charges must sum to the species charge.

Prefer smaller charge magnitudes and less charge separation; place negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom when other factors are comparable. Obey second-period octets. Formal charge divides shared electrons equally; oxidation number assigns them to the more electronegative atom. They are different bookkeeping systems.

Resonance forms describe one delocalized structure, not molecules switching back and forth. Equivalent forms contribute equally, so nitrate/carbonate have equivalent bonds with average order 4/3. Inequivalent forms do not justify a simple unweighted average; the preferred contributor matters.

sections.title: Octet exceptions
body: Incomplete octets: common for B and Be (BF₃, BeCl₂). Odd electron counts: radicals such as NO₂ cannot pair every electron. Expanded-valence Lewis structures: possible for suitable period-3 or heavier centers, such as PCl₅, SF₆, and XeF₄. C, N, O, and F do not expand their octets.
For oxyacids, H normally attaches to O. Expanded-valence drawings with fewer formal charges may be preferred by the course’s Lewis conventions, such as O=P(OH)₃.

sections.title: VSEPR: 2–4 electron groups
body: A single, double, or triple bond counts as ONE electron group. A lone pair also counts as one. Electron-group arrangement includes lone pairs; molecular shape names the positions of bonded nuclei.
2 groups: AX₂, linear, 180°. 3 groups: AX₃ trigonal planar, 120°; AX₂E bent, usually <120°. 4 groups: AX₄ tetrahedral, 109.5°; AX₃E trigonal pyramidal, usually <109.5°; AX₂E₂ bent, usually <109.5°.
Lone pairs generally repel more strongly than bonding pairs. Multiple bonds can also compress neighboring bond angles. Ideal angles are a reference, not exact values for every molecule.

sections.title: VSEPR: 5–6 electron groups
body: 5 groups: trigonal bipyramidal electron arrangement. AX₅ trigonal bipyramidal (90°, 120°, 180°); AX₄E seesaw; AX₃E₂ T-shaped; AX₂E₃ linear (180°). Lone pairs preferentially take equatorial positions, minimizing 90° interactions.

6 groups: octahedral electron arrangement. AX₆ octahedral; AX₅E square pyramidal; AX₄E₂ square planar with opposite lone pairs. Ideal bond-angle families are 90° and 180°; lone pairs can distort angles.

sections.title: Molecular polarity
body: Find the shape, then add bond dipoles as vectors. Symmetric arrangements of identical surrounding atoms can cancel: CO₂, BF₃, CCl₄, XeF₂, XeF₄, SF₆. NH₃, H₂O, SF₄, ClF₃, and BrF₅ are polar.
A shape name alone is insufficient: linear COS is polar whereas linear CO₂ is not; tetrahedral CHCl₃ is polar whereas CCl₄ is not. Do not equate “has a lone pair” with “must be polar.”

sections.title: Hybridization, overlap, and rotation
body: In the lecture’s model, 2/3/4/5/6 electron groups correspond to sp/sp²/sp³/sp³d/sp³d². The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of orbitals mixed. Hybridization is assigned locally at each center, including centers bearing lone pairs.

For course alignment, sp³d and sp³d² are used here as the slides’ labels for expanded-valence geometries; they are simplified bookkeeping models, not a claim that substantial d-orbital bonding is required in modern descriptions.

σ bonds involve end-to-end overlap; π bonds involve side-by-side overlap of parallel unhybridized p orbitals. Single = 1σ; double = 1σ + 1π; triple = 1σ + 2π. Count every bond, including C–H. A σ bond permits rotation in the simple model; a π bond restricts it because rotating destroys parallel overlap.

sections.title: Source coverage
body: Chapter 7 slides 3–23: bonding/lattice/conduction; 24–43: bond properties/electronegativity; 44–74: Lewis structures/resonance/formal charge/exceptions; 75–94: VSEPR; 95–120: hybridization and overlap. The bond-energy question supplies its equation and combines the chapter’s bond-energy objective with earlier limiting-reactant skills.

guides.title: Intermolecular forces, phase changes & phase diagrams
body: Use the new MCQ families and retained lecture-coverage questions for this chapter; the Concept / pattern filter groups three variants of each professor-review type.

sections.title: Bonding forces versus intermolecular forces
body: Intramolecular forces hold a molecule’s atoms together; intermolecular forces act between particles. Melting or boiling a molecular substance normally separates/rearranges molecules without breaking their covalent bonds. Physical behavior can change while chemical identity remains the same.

Dispersion occurs in all atoms and molecules through instantaneous and induced dipoles. Larger, more polarizable clouds usually give stronger dispersion. For similar nonpolar molecules, greater surface contact often raises boiling point; branching can lower it.

sections.title: Recognize the attractions present
body: Dipole–dipole attractions occur between polar molecules. Hydrogen bonding is a special strong dipolar interaction: an H bonded to N, O, or F interacts with an appropriate lone pair on another particle. A molecule may accept H bonds from water without donating them or hydrogen-bonding to itself (for example, an ether).

Ion–dipole attraction occurs between an ion and a polar molecule. Water’s O end points toward cations; its H ends point toward anions. Identify the actual particles present before naming their attractions.

Do not use a rigid universal ranking to compare unrelated substances. Size and polarizability can make dispersion in a large nonpolar molecule exceed attractions in a small polar molecule. Ionic solids involve ion–ion bonding, not just the molecular IMF list.

sections.title: From structure to boiling point and vapor pressure
body: For otherwise comparable substances, stronger attractions → higher boiling point and lower equilibrium vapor pressure at the same temperature. All else equal, more polarizable particles and stronger molecular dipoles increase attractions.

Molecular dipole depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles. Symmetry can cancel polar bonds. Cis-1,2-dichloroethene is polar and has a higher boiling point than its nonpolar trans isomer. Dipole moment is commonly reported in debye (D).

sections.title: States and phase changes
body: Gas: widely separated particles, high compressibility, fills the container. Liquid: close particles with mobility, nearly fixed volume, takes the container’s shape. Solid: particles localized around positions, low compressibility; they still vibrate. Thermal motion competes with attractions.

Solid → liquid: fusion/melting (+ΔH); liquid → solid: freezing (−ΔH). Liquid → gas: vaporization (+); gas → liquid: condensation (−). Solid → gas: sublimation (+); gas → solid: deposition (−). A pure substance can occupy several phases at once.

At a constant-temperature phase transition, \(q=n\Delta H_{\rm transition}\); convert mass to moles if ΔH is in kJ/mol. Reversing a phase change reverses the sign. During coexistence at fixed pressure, latent heat changes the amount of each phase rather than its temperature.

sections.title: Dynamic equilibrium and vapor pressure
body: In a closed container at liquid–vapor equilibrium, evaporation and condensation continue at equal rates. Equilibrium vapor pressure of a pure liquid depends on temperature and substance, not on how much liquid remains, provided both phases are present.

Increasing temperature increases vapor pressure. Expanding the headspace initially lowers pressure, then additional liquid evaporates to restore the same equilibrium pressure if sufficient liquid remains. If the liquid is exhausted, the remaining gas need not be saturated.

Boiling occurs when vapor pressure equals external pressure. Lower external pressure lowers the boiling temperature. The normal boiling point specifically uses 1 atm = 760 torr. Atmospheric pressure does not itself determine the pure liquid’s vapor pressure at fixed temperature.

sections.title: Clausius–Clapeyron: two temperatures
body: \(\ln(P_2/P_1)=\frac{\Delta H_{\rm vap}}{R}\left(\frac1{T_1}-\frac1{T_2}\right)\). Use Kelvin, natural log, and matching energy units: ΔHvap in J/mol with R = 8.31446 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹. Pressure units can be torr or atm, but both pressures must use the same unit.

To find a temperature: \(\frac1{T_2}=\frac1{T_1}-\frac{R}{\Delta H_{\rm vap}}\ln(P_2/P_1)\). Take the reciprocal before converting to °C. To find pressure, exponentiate the logarithm; do not multiply by the exponent.

A plot of \(\ln P\) versus \(1/T\) has slope \(-\Delta H_{\rm vap}/R\). The two-point form assumes ΔHvap is approximately constant over the temperature range. Sanity check: if T rises, vapor pressure must rise.

sections.title: Phase-diagram reading
body: Axes are pressure and temperature. Regions represent stable phases; boundaries represent two-phase coexistence. The triple point is where solid, liquid, and vapor coexist. The critical point ends the liquid–gas boundary.

Above the critical temperature, pressure alone cannot create a distinct ordinary liquid phase. Above both critical temperature and critical pressure, the substance is a supercritical fluid. Below the triple-point pressure, heating a solid can cause sublimation without a stable liquid phase.

CO₂ at 1 atm sublimes; liquid CO₂ requires suitable pressures above its triple-point pressure. Water’s solid–liquid boundary has a negative slope near ordinary conditions because liquid water is denser than ice: higher pressure favors liquid and lowers the melting point. Most substances have a positive melting-line slope.

sections.title: Connections and common mistakes
body: For gas collected over water: \(P_{\rm dry}=P_{\rm total}-P_{\rm H_2O}\), then use \(PV=nRT\) with gas-law units. A calculated water vapor pressure can be the first step in an otherwise familiar Chapter 5 problem.

Do not confuse vapor pressure with external pressure, compare vapor pressures at different temperatures without correction, omit dispersion from polar molecules, or assume an O-containing molecule must hydrogen-bond to itself.

sections.title: Source coverage
body: Chapter 8 slides 3–12: molecular polarity; 13–32: attractions and boiling-point comparisons; 33–36: phases and transition enthalpies; 37–46: equilibrium/vapor pressure/Clausius–Clapeyron/boiling; 47–49: phase diagrams. The final question combines these topics with earlier wet-gas stoichiometry; required data are supplied.

guides.title: Double Integrals over Rectangles
body: Chapter 15 turns “add up tiny contributions” into a method for two- and three-dimensional regions. The integrand describes what each piece contributes per unit area or volume; the differential describes the size of the piece. Understanding both is more important than memorizing a particular order of integration.

sections.title: From a Riemann sum to a double integral
body: Partition the rectangle \(R=[a,b]\times[c,d]\) into small rectangles. Each has area \(\Delta A=\Delta x\Delta y\). Choose a sample point in each piece, multiply the function value by its area, and add. The integral is the limit as the pieces become arbitrarily small.

For continuous functions on a closed rectangle, this limit exists. A finite midpoint approximation uses the center of each subrectangle. Do not confuse the number of sample points with the area of each piece: every sampled value must still be multiplied by \(\Delta A\).

sections.title: What the result measures
body: When \(f\ge0\) is height, the integral gives volume below the graph and above the rectangle. Negative values contribute negative signed volume. The geometric volume between a graph and the xy-plane is the integral of \(|f|\), which may require splitting the region at \(f=0\).

Units provide a useful interpretation: height in meters times area in square meters gives cubic meters; density in kilograms per square meter times area gives kilograms. Integrating a function does not automatically make the result a volume.

sections.title: Fubini’s theorem: calculate one variable at a time
body: For continuous \(f\) on \(R\), either iterated integral gives the same result.

Read from the inside out. In \(dy\,dx\), integrate with respect to y while treating x as a constant, substitute the y-limits, and then integrate the resulting function of x. After the inner integral, no y should remain. Constant bounds allow either order, but one order may make the antiderivative much easier.

sections.title: Properties that simplify the work
body: Linearity lets you split sums and pull out constants. Integrals over nonoverlapping pieces add. If \(f\le g\) throughout the region, then the integral of f is at most the integral of g. These statements concern the entire region, not just a few sample points.
For a product \(f(x,y)=g(x)h(y)\) on a rectangle, the variables separate completely.
This product rule generally fails on a nonrectangular region because the allowed values of x and y depend on one another. It also does not justify factoring a sum into a product.

sections.title: Symmetry and average value
body: An integrand odd in x integrates to zero over a region symmetric under \(x\mapsto-x\). An even integrand can allow doubling a half-region. Both the integrand and the region must have the appropriate symmetry; visual symmetry of the surface alone is insufficient.

The average value is the constant height producing the same signed volume over the same base. Divide by area, not by the length of one interval. For continuous f, this average lies between its minimum and maximum on the rectangle.

sections.title: Setup and checking routine
body: Identify the region and what f represents; select an order; carry out the inner integration with the other variable held constant; evaluate its endpoints before starting the outer integral. Finally check units, sign, symmetry, and a rough magnitude bound. A positive height over a nonzero area cannot produce a negative volume.

guides.title: Double Integrals over General Regions
body: Variable bounds encode geometry. An iterated integral is a precise instruction for sweeping through a region with line segments. Your first job is to identify where each segment enters and leaves the region.

sections.title: Type I: vertical slices
body: A Type I region has an x-interval and, for every x in that interval, a single vertical segment from a lower curve to an upper curve.

body.math: D=\{(x,y):a\le x\le b,\ g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x)\},\qquad\iint_D f\,dA=\int_a^b\!\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)}f(x,y)\,dy\,dx

body: The outer interval is the projection onto the x-axis. The inner bounds are bottom and top. A vertical slice means x is temporarily fixed while y moves; it does not mean x is integrated first.

sections.title: Type II: horizontal slices
body: A Type II region has a y-interval and horizontal slices running from a left boundary to a right boundary.

body.math: D=\{(x,y):c\le y\le d,\ h_1(y)\le x\le h_2(y)\},\qquad\iint_D f\,dA=\int_c^d\!\int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy

body: Many regions are both types. “Top minus bottom” and “right minus left” describe endpoint placement, not an extra factor to multiply into every integrand. When f is 1, integrating the inner variable automatically produces the slice length.

sections.title: Build bounds from a sketch
body: Draw and label each boundary, solve for intersection points, and determine the occupied side of every curve. Draw a representative slice away from the intersections. Trace it from entry to exit. Only then translate the picture into inequalities and an iterated integral.

An intersection gives a possible endpoint, but it does not by itself identify which curve is above the other. Check one interior point. If a boundary changes midway through the sweep, split the outer interval at that change.

sections.title: Reversing integration order
body: First recover the full region from the original inequalities. Then describe the same set with slices in the other direction. Swapping the symbols \(dx\) and \(dy\) while retaining the old bounds changes the meaning and usually produces an invalid integral.
For the region between \(y=x^2\) and \(y=x\) in the first quadrant, the two descriptions are equivalent:

body.math: 0\le x\le1,\quad x^2\le y\le x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\le y\le1,\quad y\le x\le\sqrt y

body: Solving an equation such as \(y=x^2\) for x creates two branches. The region determines which branch belongs in a bound. Here the first-quadrant restriction selects the positive branch.

sections.title: When splitting is necessary
body: A region may need several Type I or Type II pieces because a slice crosses a hole, contains disconnected intervals, or changes its entering or exiting boundary. Add integrals over pieces whose interiors do not overlap. A shared boundary contributes no area, so adjoining pieces can share endpoints.

Choose the description that balances simple bounds with an integrable inner function. Reversing order can avoid an inner antiderivative that has no elementary form. You are reorganizing the same accumulation, not changing the problem.

sections.title: Volume between surfaces and averages
body: If the solid lies above \(z=g(x,y)\) and below \(z=f(x,y)\), its vertical thickness is \(f-g\), over their actual common footprint D.

Use surface intersections to locate the footprint when appropriate. If the surfaces exchange order, split the region. Subtracting “upper minus lower” does not fix a domain that includes points outside the solid.

sections.title: Final checks
body: An inner bound may depend on the outer variable, but never on its own integration variable. After integrating the inner variable, it must disappear. Confirm that one representative slice lies inside the region and that the outer interval covers the whole projection. Symmetry shortcuts still require symmetry of both the region and the complete integrand.

guides.title: Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates
body: Polar coordinates describe a point by its distance from the origin and its direction. They are especially useful when a region or an integrand contains circles, radial symmetry, or repeated occurrences of \(x^2+y^2\).

sections.title: Coordinate dictionary
body: Theta is measured from the positive x-axis in the xy-plane. Choose an interval that covers the region once; a full revolution can use \([0,2\pi]\). Recovering theta from \(\tan\theta=y/x\) requires quadrant information. A single inverse-tangent value does not automatically describe the correct ray.

sections.title: Why the area factor is r
body: A tiny polar cell has radial thickness \(dr\) and approximate arc length \(r\,d\theta\). Its area is their product. At a larger radius, the same angular change sweeps a longer arc, so the area contribution grows.

This r comes from geometry, independently of the integrand. An integrand already containing \(x^2+y^2\) becomes \(r^2\), and then the area factor makes \(r^3\,dr\,d\theta\). Do not count the Jacobian twice or omit it because the integrand already contains r.

sections.title: Standard polar setup
body: Determine which rays meet D, then move outward along a typical ray to find the first and last allowed radii. A disk centered at the origin has \(0\le r\le a\); an annulus has \(a\le r\le b\); a sector restricts theta. A hole requires a positive lower radius.

sections.title: Translating boundaries
body: Circles centered at the origin become constant-r curves. Lines through the origin become constant-theta rays, but a full line includes opposite rays. A vertical line \(x=a\) becomes \(r\cos\theta=a\), and a horizontal line \(y=b\) becomes \(r\sin\theta=b\).

The circle \(x^2+y^2=2ax\), for \(a>0\), becomes \(r=2a\cos\theta\). Its interior can be swept using \(-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2\) and \(0\le r\le2a\cos\theta\). Restricting the angle is essential because r is nonnegative in this description.

The origin may appear as a solution before dividing by r; do not mistake it for an additional circular boundary. Intersections of radial boundary formulas determine where their ordering or role changes. Test a ray on each angular interval.

sections.title: Area, volume, and symmetry
body: This formula is just the double integral of 1 with the radial integration performed. For volume under a nonnegative graph, keep the height in the integrand. For volume between graphs, convert their difference and multiply by r.

If both the integrand and the disk or annulus are rotationally symmetric, the angular integral may simply contribute \(2\pi\). Symmetry of the region alone does not remove angular dependence from a nonsymmetric integrand such as x.

sections.title: Choosing polar intelligently
body: Polar coordinates are useful when they simplify the whole setup, not just one expression. A rectangle may acquire complicated radial bounds even if its integrand contains \(x^2+y^2\). Compare the transformed integrand and boundary complexity before committing.

Convert every x and y, every boundary, and the area element. Then check that the angular interval covers the region once and that inner radius never exceeds outer radius. The average of f over D still means its integral divided by the actual area of D, not by the area of the rectangle in the r-theta parameter plane.

guides.title: Applications of Double Integrals
body: Most applications follow the same pattern: a local contribution per unit area multiplied by a tiny area, then accumulated over the lamina. The geometry determines D; the physical quantity determines the integrand. Mass and center of mass are central in your slides. Moments of inertia and probability below expand on the textbook’s treatment.

sections.title: Density and total mass
body: A lamina is a thin plate occupying a planar region D. Its surface density \(\delta(x,y)\) has units of mass per area. The slides may use \(\rho\) for density; delta here keeps it distinct from spherical radius later.

“Density proportional to distance” requires identifying the distance: to the origin is \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\); to the x-axis is \(|y|\); to the y-axis is \(|x|\). A proportionality constant carries units and should not be silently omitted when finding mass.

sections.title: First moments and center of mass
body: The moment about the x-axis weights mass by its signed y-coordinate; the moment about the y-axis weights mass by its signed x-coordinate. This apparent reversal comes from which coordinate measures displacement from each axis.

Center of mass is a weighted average of position. More mass on one side pulls the center toward that side. It can lie outside a nonconvex plate or inside a hole; it need not be a point where material is present.

sections.title: Uniform density, centroids, and symmetry
body: For constant positive density, the constant cancels from the center-of-mass ratios. The result is the geometric centroid, obtained by replacing mass with area and density with 1.

If the shape and density are both symmetric about the y-axis, \(\bar x=0\). If only the shape is symmetric but density is larger on the right, that conclusion fails. A constant factor in density cancels in center of mass but remains in total mass and moments of inertia.

sections.title: Moments of inertia: squared distance matters
body: Moment of inertia measures how strongly mass resists angular acceleration about a specified axis. Mass farther from that axis counts more heavily, according to squared perpendicular distance.

The polar moment \(I_0\) is about the axis perpendicular to the plate through the origin. First moments use signed coordinates and can cancel; moments of inertia use squares and are nonnegative for nonnegative density. Their units are mass times length squared.

The radius of gyration about an axis is \(R=\sqrt{I/m}\). It is the distance at which all the mass could be concentrated while preserving that moment of inertia. It is generally different from the distance to the center of mass.

sections.title: Joint probability density: textbook extension
body: A joint density \(p(x,y)\) must be nonnegative and have total integral 1 over its support. Probability is accumulated density over an event region, which must be intersected with the support.

The density value at one point is not the probability of that point. In a continuous distribution, a single point has probability zero even when its density is large. A density may exceed 1 while its integral remains normalized.

body.math: E[X]=\iint xp\,dA,\qquad E[Y]=\iint yp\,dA,\qquad E[g(X,Y)]=\iint g(x,y)p\,dA

body: Expected values are the probability version of center-of-mass coordinates. For independent X and Y, the joint density factors into the product of their marginal densities. A rectangular support alone does not establish independence.

sections.title: Other accumulations and a reliable workflow
body: Charge, population, and other distributed quantities use the same integral structure with the appropriate density. Signed charge can cancel; ordinary mass density cannot be negative. Establish the support, interpret the requested quantity, choose its weight, then choose coordinates and integrate. In polar coordinates every one of these area integrals still needs the factor r.

guides.title: Surface Area
body: The area of a curved sheet is usually larger than the area of its shadow in the xy-plane. The surface-area factor measures the local stretching needed to lift a tiny flat patch onto the graph.

sections.title: A graph over a planar region
body: For a smooth graph \(z=f(x,y)\) above D, assume the partial derivatives are continuous on the relevant patch. Each point of D corresponds to one point of this graph.

This is area of the surface itself. It is not \(\iint_D f\,dA\), which represents signed volume under the graph. The actual height does not appear directly in the area formula: shifting the surface vertically changes its height but not its area.

sections.title: Where the square root comes from
body: Lifting small x- and y-directed displacements to the tangent plane gives the tangent vectors \(\langle1,0,f_x\rangle\) and \(\langle0,1,f_y\rangle\). Their cross product is \(\langle-f_x,-f_y,1\rangle\). The magnitude of that cross product gives the area stretching factor.

The factor is at least 1. A horizontal graph has factor 1; a tilted or curved graph has greater area than its projection. A plane \(z=ax+by+c\) has constant factor \(\sqrt{1+a^2+b^2}\), so its patch area equals this factor times the projected area.

sections.title: Find the correct projection first
body: D consists of the xy-points directly below the requested surface patch. Restrictions such as “inside a cylinder,” “above a rectangle,” or “below a plane” determine this footprint. If the patch ends where two surfaces intersect, substitute the graph into the other boundary to find the curve enclosing D.

For a paraboloid \(z=x^2+y^2\) cut off by \(z=h>0\), the footprint is the disk \(x^2+y^2\le h\), not a disk of radius h. Radius is \(\sqrt h\). The bounding plane sets the edge; its flat cap is a different surface and is included only if total boundary area is requested.

sections.title: Using polar coordinates for surface area
body: Compute the Cartesian partial derivatives first. Then substitute polar expressions into the square root and convert the projected area element to \(r\,dr\,d\theta\).
For \(z=x^2+y^2\), the stretching factor is \(\sqrt{1+4x^2+4y^2}=\sqrt{1+4r^2}\). The full area integrand is therefore \(\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,r\), not just the square root.

Do not replace \(f_x,f_y\) by \(f_r,f_\theta\) in the Cartesian formula: those coordinate directions have different length scales. Converting the already-correct Cartesian expression avoids that error.

sections.title: Other projection planes
body: If the patch is easier to express as a graph over yz or xz, use the corresponding formula.

Choose a projection for which the patch is single-valued and its boundaries are manageable. A whole sphere is not one graph \(z=f(x,y)\): its upper and lower halves are different branches. Add their areas or exploit justified symmetry; using only the positive square root gives only the upper hemisphere.

sections.title: Edges, checks, and scope
body: At vertical tangencies, graph derivatives may become unbounded. A different projection can help; otherwise the area integral may need an improper limit. This does not automatically mean the surface area is infinite.

Check for square-length units, a nonnegative result, and area at least as large as the chosen footprint for a single graph. Distinguish the curved patch from any additional caps or side pieces. This section concerns graph surface area; general parameterized surfaces and surface integrals appear later in Chapter 16.

guides.title: Triple Integrals
body: A triple integral accumulates contributions throughout a solid E. The geometric element is a tiny volume, not a tiny area. Most setup errors come from describing the solid incompletely or assigning a bound to the wrong stage of the integration.

sections.title: Meaning, volume, and Fubini
body: On a rectangular box, continuous functions can be integrated in any of the six orders. On a more general solid, changing order requires redescribing E and may require splitting it into pieces. The same solid and function produce the same integral whenever the applicable integrability conditions hold.

sections.title: Vertical columns over a footprint
body: For a solid between \(z=u_1(x,y)\) and \(z=u_2(x,y)\) above a planar region D, begin by integrating along each vertical column.

If \(D=\{a\le x\le b,\ g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x)\}\), the order is \(dz\,dy\,dx\). For volume, the innermost integral becomes \(u_2-u_1\), recovering the double-integral height formula. For a nonconstant f, you must actually integrate f with respect to z; multiplying f by thickness is generally invalid.

sections.title: The dependency rule for bounds
body: In \(dz\,dy\,dx\), the z-bounds may depend on x and y; the y-bounds may depend on x; and the x-bounds are constants. A bound cannot depend on the variable currently being integrated or on a variable already integrated out.
Read these bounds as a construction: choose x, then an allowed y, then move through the permitted z-segment. The outermost range alone does not describe the solid.

sections.title: The six orders and their projections
body: For \(dz\,dy\,dx\) or \(dz\,dx\,dy\), first project onto the xy-plane. For \(dy\,dz\,dx\) or \(dy\,dx\,dz\), project onto the xz-plane. For \(dx\,dz\,dy\) or \(dx\,dy\,dz\), project onto the yz-plane. The innermost variable identifies the direction of the line segment through the solid.

Changing the outermost variable produces a different family of cross-sections. Find its complete range, inspect a slice at a fixed value, then describe that two-dimensional slice with the remaining variables. This is why six orders can look very different while representing the same solid.

sections.title: A geometric setup workflow
body: Record every defining inequality, including positivity or octant restrictions. Sketch the key surfaces and their intersections. Choose an innermost direction with a simple entrance and exit. Eliminate that direction to identify the projection, then describe that projection as a double-integral region.

For a first-octant solid below \(ax+by+cz=d\) with positive coefficients, the z-column runs from 0 to \((d-ax-by)/c\). Requiring the upper endpoint to be nonnegative gives the triangular footprint \(ax+by\le d\). The footprint is not the full rectangle formed by the axis intercepts.
If some columns meet different bounding surfaces, split the projection where that change occurs. If a line passes through disconnected pieces, use separate inner intervals or another direction.

sections.title: Mass, center of mass, and averages
body: For volume density \(\delta\), mass is \(m=\iiint_E\delta\,dV\). First moments about coordinate planes are weighted by distance in the perpendicular coordinate.

body.math: \bar x=\frac{\iiint_E x\delta\,dV}{m},\qquad\bar y=\frac{\iiint_E y\delta\,dV}{m},\qquad\bar z=\frac{\iiint_E z\delta\,dV}{m}

body: Uniform density gives the solid’s centroid. Symmetry can determine a coordinate only when both the solid and density share it. The center of mass is a weighted average of position, while the average value of a general function divides its integral by volume.

sections.title: Inertia and final checks
body: Squared distance to the x-axis in space is \(y^2+z^2\), not just \(y^2\). Thus \(I_x=\iiint_E(y^2+z^2)\delta\,dV\); cyclic permutations give the other axes. This is the three-dimensional extension of the lamina formulas.

For each integral verify its dependency order, a sample column, and the projection boundaries. With nonnegative f and correctly ordered bounds, the answer is nonnegative. Volume has cubic-length units, mass has mass units, and inertia has mass times length squared.

guides.title: Triple Integrals in Cylindrical Coordinates
body: Cylindrical coordinates are polar coordinates in the xy-plane with z left unchanged. They are useful for solids organized around the z-axis: cylinders, paraboloids, cones, and circular footprints with upper and lower surfaces.

sections.title: Coordinate dictionary and volume element
body: The differential order can change when the bounds are changed appropriately. The factor r remains because the horizontal area element is polar. Here r is distance to the z-axis, whereas distance to the origin is \(\sqrt{r^2+z^2}\). Confusing these distances changes density functions and boundary equations.

sections.title: Recognizing surfaces
body: The equation \(r=a\) is a circular cylinder, \(z=c\) a horizontal plane, and \(\theta=\alpha\) a vertical half-plane through the z-axis. A full vertical plane generally involves two opposite theta values.

The paraboloid \(z=x^2+y^2\) becomes \(z=r^2\). The upper cone \(z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) becomes \(z=r\). The sphere \(x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2\) becomes \(r^2+z^2=a^2\), which still couples r and z; cylindrical coordinates do not make all spheres constant-radius surfaces.

sections.title: Standard column setup
body: Find the polar footprint, then its vertical floor and ceiling. If the solid is rotationally symmetric, the bounds often do not depend on theta, but the integrand still might. Do not multiply by \(2\pi\) until you have checked the complete transformed integrand.

sections.title: Intersections determine the footprint
body: For a solid between \(z=r^2\) and \(z=h\), their meeting radius satisfies \(r^2=h\). The vertical interval exists only for \(0\le r\le\sqrt h\). In a meridian cross-section through the z-axis, the geometry becomes a familiar two-dimensional picture of curves in r and z.

An annular footprint needs a nonzero inner radial limit. A cylinder displaced from the z-axis can have theta-dependent radial bounds. “Inside a cylinder” does not always mean a constant upper r unless its axis is the coordinate z-axis.

sections.title: Horizontal layers as an alternative
body: Sometimes z is better as an outer variable. At each fixed height, find the inner and outer radii of the horizontal cross-section. For the region above \(z=r^2\) and below \(z=h\), an equivalent description uses \(0\le z\le h\) and \(0\le r\le\sqrt z\).

This change can simplify an integrand or avoid splitting. Conversely, a shell-shaped cross-section may require a radial interval with two height-dependent endpoints. Always derive the new bounds from the solid instead of mechanically rearranging differentials.

sections.title: Applications and checks
body: For mass with density proportional to distance from the z-axis, density becomes \(kr\), and the full density-times-volume factor becomes \(kr^2\). For distance from the origin, use \(k\sqrt{r^2+z^2}\) before including the volume factor.

Check that all x and y have been converted, the r factor appears once, and theta covers the intended solid once. Choose cylindrical coordinates when circular horizontal geometry and simple z-bounds work together. If spheres and cones dominate the description, spherical coordinates may simplify it further.

guides.title: Triple Integrals in Spherical Coordinates
body: Spherical coordinates locate a point by its distance from the origin and two angles. Your course uses theta for the angle around the z-axis and phi for the angle measured down from the positive z-axis. Some sources reverse the angle names, so the geometric definitions matter more than the letters.

sections.title: Coordinate dictionary
body: Use \(\rho\ge0\), \(0\le\phi\le\pi\), and a theta interval covering at most one full revolution. The positive z-axis has \(\phi=0\), the xy-plane has \(\phi=\pi/2\), and the negative z-axis has \(\phi=\pi\). Theta does not identify an octant by itself; phi determines whether z is positive or negative.

sections.title: Why the volume factor is rho squared sine phi
body: A tiny spherical cell has approximate side lengths \(d\rho\), \(\rho\,d\phi\), and \(\rho\sin\phi\,d\theta\). Multiplying gives the local volume scaling.

The sine factor accounts for the smaller circles swept near the poles. Do not replace it with cosine because z contains cosine. The integrand and the volume element play different roles. On the standard phi range the sine is nonnegative.

sections.title: Basic regions and surfaces
body: A sphere centered at the origin is \(\rho=a\); a spherical shell lies between two constant rho values. A full ball uses \(0\le\rho\le a\), \(0\le\phi\le\pi\), and \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\). Its upper half restricts phi to \([0,\pi/2]\); its lower half uses \([\pi/2,\pi]\).

The first octant uses \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\) and \(0\le\phi\le\pi/2\). A constant phi between 0 and pi/2 describes the upper nappe of a cone; angles between pi/2 and pi describe a lower nappe. The special value pi/2 is the xy-plane.

sections.title: Cones: above and below
body: For the upper cone \(z=kr\), with \(k>0\), substitution gives \(\cot\phi=k\), so its angle is \(\phi_0=\arctan(1/k)\). Above this cone means \(z\ge kr\), hence \(0\le\phi\le\phi_0\): points closer to the positive z-axis have smaller phi.

Below that cone, if also above the xy-plane, means \(\phi_0\le\phi\le\pi/2\). Without the upper-half-space restriction, “below” can include the lower hemisphere too. Read all inequalities together. Squaring a cone equation can introduce the unwanted lower nappe unless the sign of z is retained.

sections.title: Boundaries that are not centered spheres
body: A horizontal plane \(z=h>0\) becomes \(\rho\cos\phi=h\), so its radial intersection is \(\rho=h\sec\phi\) on upward-pointing rays. This expression is not a valid positive radial endpoint on downward rays. Check which angles actually meet the surface.

The sphere \(x^2+y^2+z^2=2az\), for \(a>0\), becomes \(\rho=2a\cos\phi\). Its interior uses \(0\le\phi\le\pi/2\) and \(0\le\rho\le2a\cos\phi\). A sphere not centered at the origin usually does not give a constant radial bound.

When two radial boundaries compete, set them equal to find the switching angle. The smaller upper bound controls the inside region. If that identity changes over the angle interval, split the integral.

sections.title: A reliable setup order
body: Determine the permitted directions first: theta for azimuth, phi for tilt. Along each allowed ray, find where the solid starts and ends. Then convert the function and include the volume factor.

Density can also be denoted rho in other sections. When using spherical radius rho, write density as delta to keep the roles distinct. A density proportional to distance from the origin becomes \(k\rho\); distance from the z-axis becomes \(k\rho\sin\phi\).

sections.title: Coordinate choice and checks
body: Spheres centered at the origin and cones through the origin often favor spherical coordinates. Cylinders and paraboloids with simple floors and ceilings often favor cylindrical coordinates. Check positivity of radial bounds, the complete angular range, and the presence of both \(\rho^2\) and \(\sin\phi\). Integrating 1 over a whole ball should be consistent with \(4\pi a^3/3\).

guides.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals
body: A change of variables replaces awkward coordinates with ones adapted to the boundaries or integrand. Polar, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates are all examples of the same principle: change the function, change the region, and correct for how the transformation changes area or volume.

sections.title: Forward map and transformed region
body: Write the forward map as \(T(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v))\). Let S be the region in the uv-plane and D its image in the xy-plane. Your slides may label the new region \(R'\); the essential point is knowing which coordinates belong to which region.

The map should be differentiable and one-to-one on the relevant interior, apart from allowable boundary exceptions, with a nonzero Jacobian there for the standard substitution theorem. If several uv-points represent the same interior xy-point, integrating over all of them can count the original region multiple times.

sections.title: The Jacobian is local area scaling
body: A tiny uv-rectangle maps approximately to a parallelogram whose sides are the derivative vectors \(\langle x_u,y_u\rangle\,du\) and \(\langle x_v,y_v\rangle\,dv\). The absolute determinant is its area relative to the original rectangle. Negative determinant means orientation reverses; area itself remains nonnegative.

sections.title: Deriving the new region
body: Substitute the transformation into every boundary equation and preserve the relevant inequalities. If the original boundary is \(x+y=c\), choosing \(u=x+y\) turns it into \(u=c\). Parallel boundary families can therefore become the sides of a rectangle.

New variables may initially be defined by \(u=u(x,y)\), \(v=v(x,y)\). Solve these equations for x and y before substituting into f and calculating the forward Jacobian. Label which determinant you have actually computed.

sections.title: A linear transformation pattern
body: For \(u=x+y\), \(v=x-y\), the inverse expressions are \(x=(u+v)/2\) and \(y=(u-v)/2\). Lines of constant x+y and x-y become coordinate lines, and \(x^2-y^2=uv\). The forward determinant is \(-1/2\), so ordinary area scales by \(1/2\).

This reciprocal identity applies at corresponding points when the transformation is locally invertible. For nonlinear transformations, express the resulting factor in the variables of the final integral. A constant Jacobian is a special convenience of linear maps, not a general rule.

sections.title: Ellipses and scaled polar coordinates
body: To convert \(x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2\le1\), with positive a and b, set \(x=au\), \(y=bv\). The new region is the unit disk and the Jacobian factor is ab. If polar coordinates are then used in that disk, write \(u=s\cos\theta\), \(v=s\sin\theta\), giving the combined area factor \(ab\,s\).
Equivalently, use \(x=as\cos\theta\), \(y=bs\sin\theta\) directly. A useful substitution can simplify the boundary without simplifying every part of the integrand; assess both before proceeding.

sections.title: Three-dimensional change of variables
body: The 3-by-3 determinant has rows for x,y,z and columns for u,v,w. Geometrically, it measures the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three derivative vectors. Cylindrical coordinates have factor r; spherical coordinates have factor \(\rho^2\sin\phi\). These are not unrelated memorized corrections.

sections.title: Wedge products in your slides
body: Wedge products keep track of oriented area. They are antisymmetric: \(du\wedge dv=-dv\wedge du\), and \(du\wedge du=0\). Expanding \(dx=x_u\,du+x_v\,dv\) and \(dy=y_u\,du+y_v\,dv\) gives the determinant naturally.

This is an oriented identity. Ordinary scalar area integrals use the absolute value of the determinant. Swapping the order of an ordinary iterated area integral, while correctly changing its bounds, does not introduce a minus sign. The wedge sign and positive area measure serve different purposes.

sections.title: Chapter-wide setup checklist
body: Identify whether you are accumulating area, volume, mass, surface area, a moment, or an average. Choose coordinates based on the full geometry and integrand. Describe the transformed region completely. Transform every occurrence of the old variables, insert the correct area or volume factor exactly once, and check that the map covers the region once.

For an average, divide by the actual geometric area or volume. For surface area, include the graph stretching factor as well as any coordinate Jacobian. For density problems, distinguish the physical density from coordinate scaling. Check units, signs, symmetry, and a sample slice or ray before spending time on antiderivatives.

guides.title: How to use this review
body: The bank contains 120 MCQs: 72 new questions in 24 three-variant families, 24 curated and converted lecture-coverage questions, and all 24 questions from your supplied professor review. Original professor choices retain their original letter order. Minor wording/notation clarifications and supplied constants do not change the intended questions.

Use New Exam 2 review for the 72 variants, Retained lecture coverage for the 24 supplementary questions, and the Concept / pattern filter to practice three versions of one question type. Use Shuffle for mixed recognition. Select-all questions are explicitly labeled; select every correct statement.

Reveal answer and Answer key show final choices with a brief reason, rather than worked solutions. Select-all answers require the exact set. Choice selections, bookmarks, and reviewed status are saved in this browser. The source exam and student records are not published.

Exceptions are deliberate: Cr/Cu ground states, loss of ns before d, same-electron-count configuration exceptions, Be/B and N/O ionization exceptions, F/Cl electron affinity, octet exceptions, charged VSEPR centers, lone-pair cancellation, hydrogen-bond donors versus acceptors, and water’s negative melting-line slope. Expanded-valence sp³d/sp³d² labels follow the lecture’s simplified model.

Difficulty target: the supplied professor review plus one extra reasoning step or a plausible misconception, rather than the most difficult old integrated stoichiometry problems. The 12 earlier-chapter prerequisite questions and most elementary scaffold chains were removed from this chemistry bank.

Professor review labels identify the supplied questions. Turn off Show source labels for neutral question numbering and mixed practice. Original figure extracts retain their printed electron dots; in professor question 9 the correct panel is D, since B omits an oxygen lone pair.

sections.title: Connect the units
body: Electron configuration → valence electrons → Lewis structure → electron groups → molecular shape → dipole cancellation → intermolecular attractions → vapor pressure and boiling point. At each arrow, explain what information the next step actually needs.
Within Chapter 6: wavelength → photon energy → energy gap or electron escape; quantum numbers → orbital capacity → actual occupancy → magnetism and periodic behavior.
For each answer, explain the coefficient, unit conversion, or structural feature that made it true. Then change one condition and predict the direction of change before recalculating.

sections.title: Use the correct level of certainty
body: Two photoelectric observations bound a threshold; they need not determine every intermediate wavelength. A geometry name alone need not determine polarity. Same-temperature vapor-pressure comparisons are different from pressures measured at different temperatures.
Advanced combinations remain available, but the supplied tests were Quizzes 2–3 only. There is no claim that the added sets reproduce an unseen test’s exact topic weighting.

sections.title: Corrections retained from source review
body: The pasted radio-photon result of about 8.15 cm is consistent with its rounded constants. Quiz 2 feedback calls KNO₃ insoluble while labeling it aqueous; nitrates and potassium salts are soluble.

Equal electron counts alone are not a universal guarantee of identical configurations across arbitrary elements and excited states. For the common closed-shell main-group ions in these questions, count electrons and verify the configuration.

sections.title: File basics and locations
body:
- Files store information that remains after a program ends.
- A file extension (.txt, .csv, .pdf) suggests its format. Renaming an extension doesn’t convert the contents.
- A file object, stored in a variable, lets your program work with a file.
- A relative filename is resolved from Python’s current working directory, which is often your script’s folder.

body.code: myfile = open("data.txt", "r")

sections.title: Opening files and choosing modes

body.code: file_variable = open("filename", "mode")

body: Mode · Purpose · If the file exists · If it doesn’t exist
"r" · Read · Keeps contents · Raises an error
"w" · Write · Erases existing contents · Creates it
"a" · Append · Adds to the end · Creates it
"r+" · Read and write · Keeps existing contents · Raises an error

- Leaving out the mode defaults to "r".
- Adding "b" selects binary mode, such as "rb" or "wb".

sections.title: Closing files and using `with`
body: Close files when finished so Python releases resources and flushes buffered output.

body.code:
f = open("data.txt", "r")
text = f.read()
f.close()

body: A with block handles closing automatically, including when an error occurs:

body.code:
with open("data.txt", "r") as f:
    text = f.read()

body: After the block, text remains usable, but the file is closed.
The dot connects a method to its object: f.close() closes that particular file.

sections.title: Writing to files

body.code: f.write("some text")

body: Unlike print(), text-file write():

- Accepts one string.
- Requires numbers to be converted to strings.
- Adds no spaces or newlines automatically.

body.code:
with open("output.txt", "w") as f:
    score = 95
    f.write("Score: " + str(score) + "\n")
    f.write("Finished\n")

body: You can also use an f-string:

body.code: f.write(f"Score: {score}\n")

sections.title: Reading files and looping through lines
body: Text-file reading returns strings, even when the contents look like numbers.
Operation · Result
f.readline() · Next line as a string
f.read() · All remaining contents as one string
f.readlines() · Remaining lines as a list of strings
list(f) · Remaining lines as a list of strings
for line in f: · Processes remaining lines individually
Reading moves your position forward through the file.

- A line usually includes its ending "\n".
- readline() returns "" at the end of the file.
- A blank line is usually "\n", not "".
- Use print(line, end="") to avoid adding an extra newline.

sections.title: Splitting strings
body: split() turns a string into a list of strings using a separator.
The pieces remain strings until you convert them:

body.code: first_number = int(parts[0])

body: For a date:

body.code:
parts = "11/04/2026".split("/")
month = int(parts[0])
day = int(parts[1])
year = int(parts[2])

sections.title: Cleaning and combining strings
body: *Slide 66*

- strip() removes whitespace from the beginning and end, including spaces and newlines. It preserves internal spaces.
- join() combines strings using a chosen separator.
- Methods can be chained; operations happen from left to right.

body.code:
text = "  red,green,blue \n"
parts = text.strip().split(",")
result = "-".join(parts)
# "red-green-blue"

body: These methods return new values; they don’t change the original string.

sections.title: Putting everything together
body: A common file-processing sequence is:

1. Open the file.
2. Skip the header if present.
3. Loop through the data lines.
4. Remove surrounding whitespace.
5. Split each line into fields.
6. Convert numeric fields.
7. Store, calculate, or write the results.
For simple comma-separated data:

body.code:
# grades.csv:
# name,grade
# Alex,92
# Sam,85

grades = {}

with open("grades.csv", "r") as f:
    f.readline()                 # Skip header
    for line in f:
        parts = line.strip().split(",")
        grades[parts[0]] = float(parts[1])
